templates.title: Open pipeline at each month-end, rebuilt from field history
templates.subtopic: point-in-time reconstruction from change history, DISTINCT ON, as-of joins

sections.scenario: A sales operations team keeps its deals as opportunity records in a CRM. Each opportunity has a stage, an amount and an owner, and the CRM keeps a field history: one row per tracked field change, with the old value, the new value and when it changed. The team never took month-end snapshots, and leadership now wants the open pipeline as it stood at the end of {{months}}, by stage and owner, to compare with what was forecast at the time. You have the current records and their field history ({{opps}} opportunities, {{history_rows}} history rows).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month_end, stage, owner_id, open_opportunities, open_amount: for every month_end in report_months, the opportunities that were open at the end of that day, grouped by the stage and owner they had then, ordered by month_end, stage, owner_id. An opportunity's value of a field at a month-end is its value after every change of that field with changed_at strictly before midnight UTC on the following day. If the field had no change before then, its value was the old_value of the field's first later change, or the current value in opportunities if the field never changed. An opportunity counts only if created_at is before that midnight, and only while its stage then is not Closed Won or Closed Lost. Only the fields StageName, Amount and OwnerId matter; Amount history values are text holding whole numbers. {{fields_rule}} {{tie_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Return only groups with at least one open opportunity. A change at exactly 00:00:00 on the 1st belongs to the new month. Every field-history chain is consistent: each change's old_value is the previous change's new_value, and the last new_value is the current value.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical opportunities, owners, stages and amounts in one currency. Which fields a CRM tracks, and how it records them, is configurable and product-specific; this exercise's history table and rules are its own, so check current docs for any real product. Opportunities are never deleted in this sample.
sections.criteria: Rebuilds stage, amount and owner as of each cut-off with a strict <; falls back to the old_value of the first later change, then to the current value; excludes opportunities created after the cut-off and those closed at the time; ignores untracked fields; orders same-second changes by history_id (Very Hard); groups by the values at the time; deterministic order; can discuss snapshots versus reconstruction, currencies and history retention.

clarifications.q: An opportunity changed stage twice in May and once in June. What is its stage at the end of May?
clarifications.a: The new_value of the last May change.

clarifications.q: An opportunity's amount first changed in July. What was its amount at the end of May?
clarifications.a: The old_value of that July change: that is what the field held before it.

clarifications.q: A deal closed in May and was reopened in July. Is it in the June pipeline?
clarifications.a: No, it was closed at the end of June. It counts again at the end of July if it is open then.

clarifications.q: Which owner do I group by: the current one or the one at the time?
clarifications.a: The owner at the month-end, rebuilt the same way as the stage.

clarifications.q: A change happened at 2026-07-01 00:00:00 UTC. Is it part of the June month-end?
clarifications.a: No. Only changes strictly before midnight count.

hints: Pair every month-end with every opportunity created before its cut-off first; everything else is a lookup per (month-end, opportunity, field).

The last change before a cut-off is a DISTINCT ON (month_end, opportunity_id, field) … ORDER BY …, changed_at DESC, history_id DESC. The first change after it is the same with ascending order, and you want its old_value.
COALESCE(value before, old value after, current value) gives the value at the cut-off. Pivot the three fields with MAX(…) FILTER (WHERE field = …) before filtering closed stages.
followups: Leadership wants this every month from now on. Would you keep reconstructing from history, or start writing snapshots? What does each cost, and what does a snapshot table lose?
Amounts are entered in several currencies, and the exchange rate changes during the quarter. Which rate do you apply to a month-end amount, and why?

Field history is kept for a limited time, and older changes are archived elsewhere. How does your query behave for a month-end older than the retained history, and how would you detect that rather than silently report wrong values?
The history table holds billions of rows across many orgs. How would you index or partition it so that an as-of lookup for one org and one month stays cheap?

rules.ask: What does using the current stage do to a deal that was open at the end of May and closed in June?
A window over the history gives you changes in order. How do you get the value at a cut-off that falls between two changes, or before the first one?
A change landed at exactly midnight on the 1st. Which month does your comparison put it in?
Two changes of one field share a changed_at. Which one wins in your ordering, and is that deterministic?
If you start writing month-end snapshots today, how do you backfill the months before, and how do you make sure the backfill and the live snapshots agree?

templates.title: Lead conversion within 30 days by source, duplicates merged first
templates.subtopic: recursive CTEs, entity resolution before aggregation, cohort maturity

sections.scenario: Marketing reports, per lead source, what share of new leads convert into a customer within 30 days. The CRM is full of duplicates: the same person fills in a web form, then calls, then meets a rep at a trade show, and each time a lead record is created. Sales operations merges duplicates into one surviving lead, and the merge log keeps which lead went into which. The current report counts every lead record, so a person who arrived three times looks like two failures and one success. Rebuild it on one lead per person. The snapshot was taken at {{as_of}}; the sample has {{leads}} leads and {{merges}} merges.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns lead_source, leads, converted_30d, conversion_rate, one row per source, ordered by lead_source. First fold every merged lead into its surviving lead: a group is a surviving lead (one that was never merged into another) plus every lead merged into it. A group reports under its surviving lead's lead_source, and its start is the earliest created_at of any lead in the group. It is converted within 30 days when the surviving lead's converted_at is at or before start + 30 days (merged-away leads are never converted). Report a group only if start + 30 days is at or before {{as_of}}. leads counts groups, converted_30d the converted ones, and conversion_rate is ROUND(converted_30d / leads, 4). {{age_rule}} {{chain_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). "30 days" is exactly 30 × 24 hours: + interval '30 days' on a UTC timestamp. The boundary is inclusive. The sample is small; a production org can hold millions of leads.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical sources, leads and merges. How a real CRM merges records (which field values survive, what happens to related records) is product behaviour to check in current docs; this exercise's rule is simply that the surviving lead keeps its own values and the merged leads contribute only their creation time.
sections.criteria: Resolves every lead to its final survivor (a recursive walk for chains, Very Hard); one row per person-group; start at the earliest created_at in the group; survivor's source and conversion; inclusive 30-day boundary; immature groups excluded rather than counted as failures (Hard+); 'Unknown' for a missing source (Very Hard); rate as a rounded ratio, not integer division; deterministic order; can discuss unmerges, attribution choices and incremental resolution.

clarifications.q: Why measure from the earliest lead, not the surviving one?
clarifications.a: The person first showed interest then. Measuring from a later duplicate makes slow conversions look fast.

clarifications.q: Which source does a group report under if its duplicates came from different sources?
clarifications.a: The surviving lead's source, in this exercise. It is a choice; first-touch attribution would pick the earliest lead's source.

clarifications.q: A group's 30 days end after the snapshot. Is it unconverted?
clarifications.a: Neither. It cannot be judged yet and is not reported.

clarifications.q: Exactly 30 days after the start: in or out?
clarifications.a: In. converted_at <= start + 30 days.

clarifications.q: Can a merged-away lead have a converted_at?
clarifications.a: No, never in this sample.

hints: Resolve groups before you aggregate anything: every lead needs the id of its final surviving lead.
A survivor is a lead that never appears as merged_lead_id. A recursive CTE can walk the merge table from the survivors outwards, carrying the survivor's id as the root.
Then one aggregate per root gives the start; join the root back to leads for its source and conversion.
followups: A merge is undone a week later. How should the merge log represent that, and which past reports change?
Finance prefers first-touch attribution (the earliest lead's source) and marketing prefers the survivor's. How would you serve both without two copies of the logic?

Duplicates are only partly merged: many remain unmerged in the CRM. How would you estimate the conversion rate per person without trusting the merge log alone, and what would you report about its uncertainty?
This runs nightly for many orgs with millions of leads each. How do you make the group resolution incremental instead of recomputing every chain every night?

rules.ask: What stops your recursion if the merge table ever contained a cycle by mistake, and how would you detect one?
Distinct leads are still duplicates of one person. Which id do you count, and where in your query does a merged lead stop being a lead?
A person first arrived 40 days before converting, but the surviving record was created 10 days before. Converted within 30 days or not?
A conversion at exactly 30 days to the second: which way does your comparison decide it, and what does the specification say?
You attributed by first touch. The specification says the survivor's source; when do the two give different reports, and which would you defend to marketing?

templates.title: Case first response within entitlement, in business hours
templates.subtopic: business-time arithmetic, calendar tables, generate_series, interval intersection

sections.scenario: A support organisation runs its customer cases in a CRM. Each case has a priority, and each priority has an entitlement: a first-response target in minutes, measured on a calendar. In this exercise the business calendar is Monday to Friday, {{open_hhmm}} to {{close_hhmm}} UTC, minus the dates in holidays; time outside it does not count, so a case opened on Friday evening has not used any of its target by Monday morning. The support lead wants first-response compliance per priority as of the snapshot {{as_of}} ({{cases}} cases, {{comments}} comments).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns priority, cases, met, breached, met_rate, one row per priority with at least one judged case, ordered by priority. A case's first response is its earliest comment with author_type = 'agent' and is_public = true. Its elapsed time is the calendar time from created_at to the first response, counted on its entitlement's calendar. The case met its entitlement if elapsed time is at most response_minutes, and is breached otherwise. {{answer_rule}} {{calendar_rule}} cases = met + breached, and met_rate = ROUND(met / cases, 4).
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Measure in seconds; a response at exactly the target meets it. Timestamps are UTC; business days are UTC dates. Business hours are the half-open window [{{open_hhmm}}, {{close_hhmm}}) of each business day.
sections.assumptions: The calendar, holidays, priorities and targets are hypothetical. Real CRMs let administrators define business hours, holidays and entitlement processes in many ways; this exercise fixes one simple rule, so check current docs for any product's behaviour. Comments never predate their case.
sections.criteria: First response defined as the earliest public agent comment; business time summed per day with a correct overlap; weekends and holidays excluded; inclusive target in seconds; unanswered cases judged against the snapshot, with not-yet-due cases excluded (Hard+); a 24x7 calendar per entitlement (Very Hard); rate as a rounded ratio; deterministic order; can discuss time zones, cumulative calendar tables and clock pauses.

clarifications.q: A case arrives on Saturday. When does its clock start?
clarifications.a: Effectively at the next business opening: no time counts until then.

clarifications.q: An agent replies at 21:00 on a weekday. How much business time has passed since 17:00?
clarifications.a: None. Business time stops at closing; the reply at 21:00 has the same elapsed time as a reply at closing.

clarifications.q: Does an automatic "we received your case" email count as the first response?
clarifications.a: No. Only a public comment by an agent.

clarifications.q: Is a response at exactly the target met or breached?
clarifications.a: Met.

clarifications.q: Does a holiday that falls on a weekend matter?
clarifications.a: No holiday in this sample falls on a weekend; a holiday removes a business day.

hints: Business time between two instants is a sum over calendar days: for each business day, the overlap of [created, response] with [day + open, day + close].

generate_series(date_trunc('day', s), date_trunc('day', t), interval '1 day') gives the days; filter weekends with EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d) < 6 and holidays with an anti-join; LEAST/GREATEST give the overlap, kept only when positive.
Decide each case's fate (met, breached, not judged) in one CTE, then aggregate with COUNT(*) FILTER (…).
followups: Customers are in several time zones and each support region has its own business hours. What changes in the data model and in the query?
At millions of cases, generating a row per case-day is expensive. Precompute a cumulative business-seconds table per calendar so that elapsed time is two lookups and a subtraction. Sketch it.
The entitlement clock should pause while the case waits on the customer. How would you model status intervals, and how do pauses combine with business hours?
The dashboard must show live time-to-breach for open cases every minute. Which parts of your query move into a stream, and which stay batch?

rules.ask: That subtraction counts nights and weekends. A case opened Friday at 18:00 and answered Monday at 09:30: how much business time is that?
How many rows does your series produce for a case that stayed open for a year, and how would you avoid generating them?
The holiday calendar changes after the fact (a regional holiday added late). Which past results change, and do you recompute them?
What would happen to the report if you dropped this filter, and which kind of comment is most likely to appear first?
An unanswered case is still within its target at the snapshot. Why is it neither met nor breached, and what bias appears if you count it either way?

templates.title: Records each user can see through the role hierarchy
templates.subtopic: iterative post-order aggregation, subtree sums, forests

sections.scenario: In a multi-tenant CRM an org arranges its users in a role hierarchy: a sales VP above regional directors, above managers, above reps. One common way such systems share records is upward: a user can see the records owned by users in roles below their own. An admin team wants to audit an org's sharing before a reorganisation and asks, for every user, how many records the hierarchy lets them see. The org is large, and its hierarchy, imported from a territory model, can be very deep.
sections.problem: Implement visible_counts(roles, users, records, no_hierarchy). roles lists (role_id, parent_role_id), with None for a top-level role; the roles form a forest. users lists (user_id, role_id). records lists (record_id, object_name, owner_user_id). Under this exercise's rule a user can see (a) every record they own, and (b) every record owned by a user whose role is strictly below theirs: a child role, a grandchild role, and so on. Users in the same role do not see each other's records through the hierarchy. Return {user_id: number of visible records} for every user, including users who see nothing. {{role_rule}} {{object_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 12 000 roles, 30 000 users and 120 000 records; the hierarchy can be thousands of levels deep, so recursion depth is a real limit in CPython. Every owner is a listed user and every parent a listed role; there are no cycles. Expected: O(roles + users + records). Walking each user's (or each role's) subtree is too slow on a deep tree.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical orgs, roles and records. Real CRM sharing combines org-wide defaults, role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams and manual shares, and its exact behaviour is configurable; this exercise uses only the hierarchy rule above, so check current docs for any product. Each record counts once per user even if two rules would grant it.
sections.criteria: Separates "own records" from "records strictly below the role"; aggregates per role, not per user; an iterative post-order (or reverse pre-order) sum that survives deep trees; handles forests, empty roles and users with zero records; users without a role see only their own (Hard+); objects excluded from hierarchy sharing still count for their owner (Very Hard); O(n); can discuss per-record queries, sharing rules and incremental reorganisation.

clarifications.q: Two reps share the role "Team A". Does one see the other's records?
clarifications.a: Not through the hierarchy. Only roles strictly below yours.

clarifications.q: My manager's manager is two roles up. Does she see my records?
clarifications.a: Yes. Every ancestor role sees them.

clarifications.q: A role has no users but has roles below it. Does it matter?
clarifications.a: It has no one to show the count to, but the records below it still count for every role above it.

clarifications.q: Do I return users who see nothing?
clarifications.a: Yes, with 0.

clarifications.q: Can I use recursion?
clarifications.a: The tree can be thousands of levels deep; Python's default recursion limit is about 1 000. Use an explicit stack.

hints: A user's count is their own records plus the records owned strictly below their role. The second part depends only on the role, not the user.
Count shareable records per role first (owned by users in exactly that role). Then the total at or below a role is its own count plus its children's totals: a post-order sum.
Build a parents-first order with an explicit stack from the roots; walking it in reverse visits every child before its parent. Below-role = subtree total − the role's own count.
followups: The audit now needs the list of users who can see one particular record, not counts. How would you answer that per record without precomputing everything?
Sharing rules add "role R and its subordinates can see records owned by role Q and its subordinates". How do you extend the computation, and how do you avoid double counting a record granted twice?
A reorganisation moves one role (with its subtree) under a different parent. Which counts change, and can you update them without recomputing the whole tree?

This audit runs across many thousands of orgs every night. How would you structure the job so that one huge org does not dominate, and what do you store so a support engineer can explain one user's count?

rules.ask: The test hierarchy is about 6 000 levels deep. What happens to your recursive function at depth 1 000, and what do you change?
How many tree nodes does your loop visit in total when the tree is one long chain, and how do you make it linear?
How does your code make sure peers in one role do not count each other's records, while their manager counts both?
Holding a set of record ids per role is O(roles × records) memory on a deep tree. Do you need the sets, or only the counts?
Caching per role removes repeated work across users of one role, but what is still repeated between a role and its parent?

templates.title: Routing each case to the agent with the most spare capacity
templates.subtopic: priority queues with lazy invalidation, per-key heaps, event processing

sections.scenario: A contact centre built on a cloud CRM pushes incoming work (cases, chats, messages) to agents instead of letting agents pick from a queue. Each agent has skills and a capacity: how many units of work they can hold at once. The team is testing a "most available" policy: send each new case to the agent with the skill who has the most spare capacity, so load spreads evenly. Before turning it on, they want to replay a day of traffic and see exactly where every case would have gone.
sections.problem: Implement route_cases(agents, events). agents lists (agent_id, skills, capacity). events are processed in list order (their times never decrease): ('case', t, case_id, skill, units) asks for routing; ('done', t, case_id) completes a routed case and frees its units; ('offline', t, agent_id) and ('online', t, agent_id) change presence. Under this exercise's rule a case goes to an online agent who has skill and whose spare capacity (capacity minus units of their cases not yet done) is at least units; among them, the one with the most spare capacity; ties go to the agent whose latest assignment is oldest (an agent never assigned counts as oldest of all), then to the agent listed first in agents. If no agent qualifies, the case gets None (it overflows to a queue outside this exercise) and is never routed later. A 'done' for a case that was never routed is ignored. Return {case_id: agent_id or None} for every case. {{units_rule}} {{done_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 2 000 agents, hundreds per skill, and 60 000 cases with as many completions. Times are non-negative integers. Expected: O(E · k · log E) for E events and k skills per agent. Scanning every agent with the skill for every case is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical agents, skills, capacities and traffic. Real routing products offer several documented policies (for example least-active or most-available, with their own tie-breaks, queues and push timeouts); this exercise's rule is its own, so check current docs for any product. Routing is instantaneous and an agent never declines work.
sections.criteria: Picks the most spare capacity among online agents with the skill, then the oldest latest assignment (never assigned first), then input order; frees capacity only for routed cases; one heap per skill with lazy invalidation, so agents with several skills stay consistent; the top-entry test for "nobody fits"; units and presence (Very Hard); O(E log E); can discuss waiting queues, alternative policies and concurrency across routing servers.

clarifications.q: Agent A has 3 spare units and B has 2. A case needs 1 unit. Who gets it?
clarifications.a: A, the most spare capacity, even if B is listed first.

clarifications.q: Both have 2 spare. A was last assigned at t = 50, B at t = 80. Who gets it?
clarifications.a: A: the latest assignment that is oldest. An agent never assigned beats both.

clarifications.q: A case needs 2 units; two agents each have 1 spare. Can it be split?
clarifications.a: No. It goes to one agent with at least 2 spare, or to nobody.

clarifications.q: An agent goes offline while holding cases. What happens to them?
clarifications.a: They stay with the agent and still complete; the agent just gets nothing new until back online.

clarifications.q: When an agent has no room, does the case wait for them?
clarifications.a: No. It gets None at once and never routes later.

hints: The best agent for a skill is a maximum over a changing set: keep one heap per skill keyed by (-spare, last_assigned, input position).

An agent's key changes on every assignment, completion and presence change, and an agent with two skills sits in two heaps. Instead of updating heap entries, push a fresh entry and bump a version number; skip entries whose version is out of date when they reach the top.
Once the top valid entry cannot fit the case, nobody can: it has the most spare capacity.
followups: Instead of overflowing, unroutable cases now wait in a queue per skill and are pushed when capacity frees up. Which agent's completion should pull which waiting case, and what changes in your structures?

Product wants "least active" instead: the agent with the fewest units in progress, regardless of capacity. Show a sequence where the two policies send a case to different agents, and say which spreads load better.
Agents have a skill level from 1 to 10 and a case needs at least level L. How would you index agents so that "most spare capacity among those with level ≥ L" stays fast?
Many routing servers share the same agents. How do you keep two servers from giving the same last unit of capacity to two cases?

rules.ask: Hundreds of agents share a skill and every case changes one of them. What does sorting or scanning per case cost over 60 000 cases?
An agent with two skills changes load. How do you update both heaps without searching for the old entries?
How large can a heap grow with stale entries, and when would you rebuild it?
The rule is most spare capacity first, and idleness only breaks ties. Where in your key does each appear?
Can a 2-unit case be split across two agents with 1 spare each under this rule? What does your code return?

templates.title: Formula field recalculation order after a record save
templates.subtopic: dependency levels, reverse reachability, cycle detection

sections.scenario: A CRM lets each customer org define formula fields on its objects: Net_Amount__c reads Amount and Discount__c, Commission__c reads Net_Amount__c, and so on. A reporting cache stores the value of every formula field next to the record, so reports and search can filter on them without computing formulas on every read. When a record is saved, the cache must recompute exactly the formula fields whose value can have changed, and it must compute each one after every formula it reads. You are writing the planner that turns a save into that list.
sections.problem: Implement recalc_order(formulas, edits). formulas maps each formula field's API name to the list of field names its expression reads. A name that is not a key of formulas is an ordinary input field. edits is a list of record saves, and each save is a list of the input fields it changed. For each save, return the formula fields that read a changed field directly or through other formula fields, in evaluation order. This exercise's evaluation order is by level, then by API name in plain string order. A formula that reads no formula fields has level 1. Any other formula has level 1 + the highest level among the formula fields it reads. Levels are computed over all of formulas, not only over the fields a save affects. Return one list per save, in the order of edits. If the formulas contain a cycle anywhere, including a formula that reads itself, the configuration is invalid: return None. {{shape_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 formula fields, 150 000 references and 5 000 saves. Computing levels once in O(V + E) and then, for each save, touching only the affected formulas and their references (plus sorting them) is expected. Re-evaluating every formula until nothing changes, for every save, is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Field names, objects and sizes are hypothetical. The level rule and the cycle rule are this exercise's; check current docs for how a real platform evaluates formulas and rejects circular references. Edits name only input fields. A formula's value depends only on the fields it lists.
sections.criteria: Affected set exactly the formulas reachable from the edited fields; levels computed over the whole configuration as the longest chain, not the distance from the edit; order by (level, name); None for any cycle, including a self-reference and a cycle no save reaches; repeated references and unknown names handled; one list per save including empty ones; levels computed once and only affected formulas touched per save, with the complexity stated; sensible answers on cross-object formulas, early cut-off and metadata changes.

clarifications.q: Does an edited field appear in the output?
clarifications.a: No. Only formula fields are recalculated, and edits only name input fields.

clarifications.q: Why level and then name, rather than any valid topological order?
clarifications.a: So that the answer is unique and two runs of the cache log the same order. Any order by level is a valid evaluation order, because a formula's inputs all have lower levels.

clarifications.q: Is the level measured from the edited field?
clarifications.a: No. It is a property of the formula in the whole configuration: the longest chain of formula references below it.

clarifications.q: A formula reads a field that no formula defines and that is not on the object as far as I know.
clarifications.a: Treat every name that is not a key of formulas as an input field.

clarifications.q: The cycle is between two fields that no save touches. Is that still None?
clarifications.a: Yes. A configuration with a cycle is rejected as a whole, whatever the saves are.

clarifications.q: Can a formula list the same field twice?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example IF(Discount__c > 0, Amount * Discount__c, 0). It still reads the field once for this purpose.

hints: Build the reverse map once: for every field, the formulas that read it. A save's affected set is everything reachable from its fields in that map.
Kahn's algorithm processed layer by layer gives every formula its level and detects a cycle in the same pass: formulas that never reach in-degree zero are on a cycle or behind one.
Count a formula's distinct formula inputs when you compute in-degrees, or a repeated reference will hold it back for ever.
followups: Formulas can read a parent record's fields, such as Account.Industry on an opportunity. A save on one account must recalculate formulas on 30 000 child opportunities. What changes in your plan and in its cost?
A save changes Amount but the recomputed Net_Amount__c comes out unchanged. How would you stop the recalculation from continuing past it, and what does that do to your precomputed order?
An administrator edits one formula in a configuration of 50 000. How do you update levels without recomputing them all, and when can a single edit change the level of thousands of fields?
Saves arrive at 20 000 a second across thousands of orgs, each with its own formulas. Where do you cache the plan, and how is it invalidated when an org deploys new metadata?

rules.ask: A chain of 20 000 formulas each reading the one before is legal here. What happens to your recursion in CPython, and how would you write it without recursion?
How many passes over all 50 000 formulas does one save take in the worst case, and how many saves are there?
A formula reads the edited field directly and also reads a formula two levels up. Which level does your code give it, and does it run after both of its inputs?
Your walk marks fields as seen. Where do you clear that set between saves, and what is the cost of clearing it?
What is the key of your cache, and what happens to it when the org changes one formula?

templates.title: Matching new leads to accounts by email domain
templates.subtopic: label-wise suffix lookup, normalisation, ambiguity

sections.scenario: Leads arrive in a CRM from web forms, events and purchased lists, each with an email address. Sales wants every lead from a company the org already sells to routed to that company's account owner, so a matching step links each new lead to an account by the domain of its email. Large customers have several domains and regional subdomains, and a regional subsidiary may be its own account under a subdomain of its parent's domain. Leads from personal email providers must never be matched, and a domain that two accounts both claim must go to a person rather than to a guess.
sections.problem: Implement match_leads(accounts, leads, public_domains). accounts is a list of (account_id, domains), leads a list of email strings and public_domains a list of personal email domains. Compare everything after removing surrounding spaces and lowercasing. A lead's domain is the text after the last @. A lead with no @, or with nothing after it, matches nothing. A lead whose domain equals a public domain or ends with . followed by one matches nothing. Otherwise an account domain matches the lead if it equals the lead's domain or the lead's domain ends with . followed by it, so sales.acme.com matches acme.com but notacme.com does not. Of the matching account domains, the longest wins. If that domain is listed by more than one account, the lead is ambiguous and matches nothing; do not fall back to a shorter domain. Return, for each lead in order, the winning account_id or None. {{data_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 accounts with up to five domains each, and 500 000 leads in a batch. Work per lead should depend on the number of labels in its domain, not on the number of accounts. Comparing every lead with every account domain is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Accounts, domains, people and the public list are hypothetical. The matching rules are this exercise's; check current docs for how a real duplicate or matching rule behaves. Domains contain only letters, digits, hyphens and dots, and no domain starts or ends with a dot. An account listing the same domain twice still claims it once.
sections.criteria: Normalisation of emails, account domains and public domains; domain taken after the last @ and malformed emails rejected; label-boundary suffix matching; public domains and their subdomains never matched, even if an account lists one; the longest matching domain wins and an ambiguous longest domain gives None with no fallback; duplicates within one account not counted as ambiguity; per-lead work proportional to labels; clear answers on freshness, related country domains and multi-tenancy.

clarifications.q: Does www.acme.com match an account that lists acme.com?
clarifications.a: Yes, like any other subdomain. The match is on whole labels from the right.

clarifications.q: A public domain is also listed by an account, because somebody typed it in. What happens?
clarifications.a: The lead matches nothing. The public list always wins.

clarifications.q: Two accounts list emea.acme.com and a third lists acme.com. A lead comes from eu.emea.acme.com.
clarifications.a: None. The longest matching domain is ambiguous, and an ambiguous lead goes to a person, not to the parent account.

clarifications.q: Why the last @?
clarifications.a: A quoted local part can contain @, as in "pat@home"@acme.com. The domain is always after the last one.

clarifications.q: Should I validate the domain further, for example its top-level domain?
clarifications.a: No. Apply only the rules in the statement.

hints: Put every account domain in a dict from domain to the set of accounts that list it. Then a lead needs only the suffixes of its own domain.
The suffixes of a.b.c.com that end on a label boundary are a.b.c.com, b.c.com, c.com and com. Walk them from longest to shortest and stop at the first one an account claims.
The public check uses the same suffixes. Decide whether it can stop at the first claimed suffix, or has to look at all of them.
followups: The batch is 500 000 leads and the accounts change all day. How do you keep the domain dict fresh without rebuilding it for every batch?
Country-code domains such as acme.co.uk and acme.com.au belong to the same group. How would you link them, and who should be allowed to say they are one company?

Sales wants a confidence score instead of a yes or no, and to send ambiguous leads to the account owner with the most open opportunities. What would you need to log to know whether that is a good idea?
The same matching must run inside many customer orgs, each with its own accounts. What is shared between orgs, and what must never be?

rules.ask: notacme.com ends with acme.com. Show the line in your code that stops that match.
A dict of full domains also works here. What does your trie buy you, and what does it cost in memory for 500 000 domains?
What does your code do with "pat@home"@acme.com, and with an address that has no @ at all?
How many patterns does your regex try per lead, and how does that grow with the number of accounts?
Two accounts claim the regional domain. Who should get the lead, and why is sending it to the parent account risky?

templates.title: Debug the forecast rollup
templates.subtopic: forecast categories, splits, dated rates, fiscal calendars, ownership

sections.scenario: Sales leaders review a forecast every week: for each rep and fiscal quarter, how much is closed, committed, at best case and in the pipeline, all in the company's corporate currency. A job rebuilds the rollup from opportunities, opportunity splits and dated exchange rates. Since the last release the sales operations team has raised five complaints. Deals reps have marked Omitted still inflate the pipeline. A euro deal that closed on the day a new rate took effect was converted at the old rate. On split deals only one member of the team sees any credit. Some reassigned deals still count for the rep who handed them over. With a fiscal year that starts in February, deals closing in February land in the wrong fiscal year. The function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix forecast_rollup(opps, split_rows, rates, corporate, fy_start) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Opportunities. Each is {"id", "owner_history", "amount", "currency", "close_date", "category"}. amount is an integer in the currency's minor units, and close_date is "YYYY-MM-DD". owner_history is a list of (date, user) ownership changes in no particular order, with distinct dates. The owner is the user of the change with the latest date, so a deal reassigned in the middle of a quarter counts entirely for its new owner.
  2. Credit. If split_rows has rows (opp_id, user, percent) for an opportunity, every one of those users is credited with their percent (the percents sum to 100). Otherwise the owner is credited with 100.
  3. Currency. An opportunity in the corporate currency converts at exactly 1. Otherwise use the rate (currency, effective_date, ppm) for its currency with the latest effective_date on or before close_date. ppm is corporate units per 1 000 000 units of the currency. Each credited amount is amount * percent * ppm // 100_000_000, rounded down per credited user. Rates are not sorted. There is at most one rate per currency and date, and one always exists on or before a close date.
  4. Fiscal quarter. The fiscal year starts on the first day of month fy_start (1–12) and is named by the calendar year in which it ends, so with fy_start = 2 a deal closing on 10 February 2026 is in FY2027-Q1. Quarter 1 is the first three months of the fiscal year.
  5. Categories. This exercise's rollup is cumulative: Closed counts in closed, commit, best_case and pipeline; Commit in commit, best_case and pipeline; Best Case in best_case and pipeline; Pipeline in pipeline; Omitted in none.
  6. Output. {"<user>/FY<year>-Q<n>": {"closed", "commit", "best_case", "pipeline"}} with a row for every user and quarter credited by at least one opportunity, Omitted ones included (a rep whose only deal is Omitted shows a row of zeros).
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 opportunities and 50 000 rates, in O((n + r) log r).
sections.assumptions: Opportunities, rates and calendars are hypothetical. Forecast categories, cumulative rollups, split credit, dated rates and fiscal-year naming are this exercise's rules; check current docs for how a real forecasting feature is configured. Amounts are never negative.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; Omitted counts nowhere but keeps its row; the rate effective on the close date applies; every split member is credited and rounded down separately; the owner is the latest change by date; the first month of a fiscal year belongs to the new fiscal year; minimal fixes that keep the complexity; a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Which rate applies when the rate changes on the close date itself?
clarifications.a: The new one. A rate effective on the close date is "on or before" it.

clarifications.q: Does a deal reassigned mid-quarter split its amount between the two owners?
clarifications.a: No. The whole deal counts for the current owner, the user of the latest change.

clarifications.q: When a deal has splits, does the owner get anything extra?
clarifications.a: Only if the owner is one of the split rows.

clarifications.q: Why does an Omitted deal create a row at all?
clarifications.a: So a manager can see that a rep has deals in the quarter, even if all of them are Omitted. The row's numbers are zero unless other deals add to them.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: For each complaint, write the smallest input that reproduces it: one opportunity is usually enough.
Read the rate lookup at its boundary: the rate list for EUR is ["2026-01-01", "2026-04-01"] and the deal closes on 2026-04-01. Which index does bisect_left return, and which does bisect_right?
Look at every place the code builds a dict from rows, and ask what happens when two rows share a key.
Write out the fiscal year for every month with fy_start = 2, and compare with the rule.
followups: Finance wants last quarter's forecast reproduced exactly as it was on the Friday it was reviewed, even though deals, owners and rates have changed since. What would you store?
Rates for a currency arrive a week late. Which rows change when they arrive, and how do you tell the sales leaders?
Splits that do not sum to 100 appear after a data import. What would you do with them, and where would you check?
The rollup runs for thousands of orgs with different fiscal calendars, including custom calendars with 13 periods. What would you change in the fiscal-quarter logic?

rules.ask: Where could a fraction of a cent appear in your fix, and which rounding rule does the specification ask for?
Two ownership changes on the same date would make "latest" ambiguous. What would you ask the data owner to add?
Why does the specification tie the rate to the close date, and what would a leader see each week if you used today's rate?
Which other dict in this function is built from rows that can share a key, and is it safe?
With a fiscal year that starts in November, which quarter is January in, and which fiscal year?

templates.title: Ingesting many sources into a customer data platform
templates.subtopic: connectors, mapping to a common model, freshness per source, multi-tenant ingestion

sections.scenario: A customer data platform is offered to {{tenants}} customer orgs. Each org connects its own sources: the CRM's own objects, an online store, a mobile app's event stream, a marketing email tool, files dropped in cloud storage, and tables in the org's data warehouse. Together they bring in about {{daily_records}} records a day. Each org maps its sources onto a common data model (individuals, contact points such as email and phone, orders, engagement events) so that segmentation, identity resolution and analytics downstream can read one shape. Streaming sources should be queryable within {{fast_freshness}}; batch sources such as file drops and warehouse tables within {{batch_freshness}} of their arrival.
sections.problem: Design the ingestion layer up to the common model. Cover the connector framework (push and pull, full and incremental extracts, credentials, retries), how raw data lands and is kept, how each org's field mappings and transformations are stored, versioned and applied, schema changes at the source, deletions at the source, how freshness is measured and reported per source, isolation between orgs on shared infrastructure, and what an org administrator sees when a source is late or broken. Identity resolution and segmentation are downstream; describe only what you hand to them.
sections.constraints: One org's data must never be visible to another, and a large org's backfill must not delay a small org's stream. A source can redeliver a file or replay a stream, and the result must not double count. A change to an org's mapping must be reproducible: you must be able to say which mapping version produced any record in the common model. A deletion in a source must reach the common model within a day.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, freshness targets and source types are hypothetical. Connector behaviours and limits are this exercise's; check current docs for any real product. Each source delivers either change events with a key and a timestamp, or periodic full extracts. The platform runs on shared compute with a shared object store and a lakehouse table format.
sections.criteria: Connectors with clear incremental semantics and idempotent landing (file hash, source key and version); raw data kept immutable per org; mappings stored and versioned, every row stamped with its mapping version; replay from raw for remaps; schema changes detected and surfaced, not silently nulled; deletions handled both from explicit events and from absence, with a guard against truncated extracts; freshness measured per source and org and shown to administrators; fair sharing and quotas so one org cannot delay others; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Does the common model have fixed fields?
clarifications.a: It has standard objects and fields, and orgs may add custom fields to them. Mappings are per org and per source.

clarifications.q: How does a full extract tell you about deletions?
clarifications.a: Only by absence: a key in yesterday's extract and not in today's. Some sources also send explicit delete events.

clarifications.q: What does freshness mean for a batch source?
clarifications.a: The time from a file's arrival in the drop location to its rows being queryable in the common model. For streams, from the event's ingestion time.

clarifications.q: Who writes the mappings?
clarifications.a: Org administrators in a configuration screen. They change them at any time, and sometimes get them wrong.

clarifications.q: Can two sources write the same common-model record?
clarifications.a: Yes, two sources can describe the same order. Keep both, with their source; reconciling them is downstream.

hints: Land everything raw, immutable and per org before mapping it. Remapping then means replaying from raw data, not asking the source again.
Make each common-model row carry its source, the source key, the source's own timestamp and the mapping version that produced it.
Measure freshness from the source's point of view, per source and per org, and publish it, not only an internal queue lag.
followups: An administrator fixes a wrong mapping that has been live for two weeks. What do you reprocess, how long does it take for an org at {{daily_records}} a day, and what do downstream consumers see meanwhile?
A source adds a column, renames another and changes a date format, all without notice. What does each stage do?
A full extract arrives with 40% fewer rows than yesterday's. Do you treat the missing keys as deletions?
One org starts a backfill of five years of order history. How do you keep every other org inside {{fast_freshness}}?
How would you show an org administrator that a deletion requested in the source has reached every table you manage?

rules.ask: What is your partition key, and what happens to the other orgs on that partition when one org replays a month of events?
The source renames a field your mapping uses. Does ingestion stop, write nulls, or keep the old name, and who finds out?
A source replays yesterday's events after a fix. How does your merge decide which version of a record wins?
A file is truncated in transit. What stops your pipeline from deleting half of the org's customers?
Downstream asks why one customer's email changed last Tuesday. What can you show them, record by record?

incidents: A partner's file drop delivers yesterday's file again, with a new name, for 300 orgs at once; freshness looks fine but the row counts double for some orgs.
One org's warehouse connector backfill reads {{daily_records}} worth of history in an afternoon, and stream freshness for other orgs slips past {{fast_freshness}}.
An administrator saves a mapping that sends the phone column into the email field; within an hour, downstream identity resolution starts merging profiles on phone numbers.

templates.title: Flow automation telemetry — runs, faults and the chain one save sets off
templates.subtopic: execution traces, causal chains, element timings, tenant-safe telemetry

sections.scenario: A CRM lets administrators build automations without code: record-triggered flows that run before or after a record is saved, scheduled flows, and flows started by platform events. One save can set off a chain: a flow on an opportunity updates its account, which triggers the account's flow, which creates a task, which triggers another flow, some of it in the same transaction and some on asynchronous paths later. Across {{orgs}} orgs there are about {{daily_runs}} flow runs a day. Administrators ask "why did this record change?", "which flow failed and why?" and "which element makes saves on this object slow?". This exercise's platform stops a chain deeper than {{max_depth}} levels and enforces per-transaction limits on queries and record updates.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry pipeline for flow runs. Cover what each run emits (run, element and fault events, timings, the limits it used), how runs in one save are tied together into a chain across synchronous and asynchronous steps, where the telemetry is produced so it does not slow the save, how it is transported, stored and aggregated, what is kept in detail and for how long ({{detail_retention}} in detail, aggregates longer), the views an administrator gets for one record, one flow and the whole org, and how you make sure no record field values from the customer's data leak into telemetry or across orgs.
sections.constraints: Telemetry must never fail or noticeably slow a save; if the pipeline is behind, runs still execute. An administrator sees only their own org. Field values are customer data and are not recorded by default; record ids are. Some chains finish in milliseconds and others continue for hours through asynchronous steps. Costs scale with {{daily_runs}} runs a day, most of which succeed in under 100 ms.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, depth limits, retention periods and per-transaction limits are hypothetical and this exercise's own; check current docs for how a real automation platform records runs and enforces limits. Each run has a flow id, a flow version, an org id, the triggering record id and an element-by-element path.
sections.criteria: Run, element and fault events with flow version, org, record id and limit use, and no field values by default; chain and parent ids that carry across synchronous and asynchronous steps; non-blocking emission with bounded buffers and counted drops; tiered storage with {{detail_retention}} of detail and longer aggregates; sampling that keeps faults and slow runs and exact aggregate counts; per-org isolation in storage and queries with quotas against noisy orgs; administrator views for a record, a flow and an org; time-boxed, audited value capture; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Do I store every element of every successful run?
clarifications.a: You decide, and justify it with the cost at {{daily_runs}} runs a day. Failed runs must be kept in full detail.

clarifications.q: What ties an asynchronous step to the save that caused it?
clarifications.a: Nothing yet. You design the identifiers that carry the chain across steps.

clarifications.q: Can an administrator turn on extra detail, such as field values, for debugging?
clarifications.a: Yes, for one flow or user for a limited time, with an audit record. Default telemetry never has values.

clarifications.q: What does "the chain one save sets off" include?
clarifications.a: Every flow run caused directly or indirectly by that save, in this transaction or later asynchronous steps, with the record each one changed.

clarifications.q: How fast must a failure show up?
clarifications.a: An administrator watching a failing flow should see the fault within a minute.

hints: Give every save a chain id and every run a run id and a parent run id; pass them through asynchronous work the same way a distributed trace passes its context.
Buffer telemetry in memory on the application server and ship it asynchronously, with a bounded buffer and counted drops, so a slow pipeline costs data, not saves.
Decide on sampling per outcome: keep all faults and slow runs, sample fast successes, and keep exact counts in aggregates regardless.
followups: An administrator asks why an account's rating changed at 10:42 yesterday. Walk through the query and the data that answers it.
A flow fails one run in a thousand, only for records owned by one queue. How do your aggregates make that visible, and what detail do you need?
One org's flows loop until they hit the {{max_depth}}-level limit thousands of times an hour. What does your pipeline do with that volume, and what do you tell the administrator?
You sample fast successful runs. How do you still report an exact run count and an accurate p95 duration per flow?
A flow version is deployed from a sandbox. How do you compare its timings and fault rate with the previous version fairly?

rules.ask: The telemetry store is slow for ten minutes. What happens to every save in every org during those ten minutes?
Which runs are never sampled out, and how do you correct the counts and percentiles for the ones that are?
How does your id survive a step that is queued and runs two hours later on another server?
Whose data is that, who can see it in your store, and how long do you keep it?
How do you stop one org's runaway loop from filling the storage and query capacity every other org shares?

incidents: A loop in one org's flows produces 30% of all runs for an hour, every chain stopping at the {{max_depth}}-level limit.
The telemetry buffer fills during a storage outage, and four minutes of successful-run events are dropped; the next day an administrator asks for a run in that window.
An administrator's debugging session captured field values for one flow and was never switched off; three weeks later the values are still being recorded.

templates.title: Who could see this record on that date — the sharing model as data
templates.subtopic: temporal access policy, role and group closure, derived access with reasons

sections.scenario: In a multi-tenant CRM each customer org controls who can see its records. In this exercise's rules (check current docs for the product's own): an organisation-wide default per object (Private, Public Read Only or Public Read/Write) sets the baseline; a record's owner has full access; users whose role sits above the owner's role in the org's role hierarchy get the owner's access, for objects where hierarchy access is switched on; sharing rules grant Read Only or Read/Write to a group or a role, either for records owned by members of another group or role (owner-based) or for records whose fields match criteria (criteria-based); an owner can share one record manually with a user or group; and record teams give their members an access level on one record. Public groups can contain users, roles, "roles and subordinates" and other groups. Every mechanism only widens access beyond the default. One large org here has {{org_records}} records, a role hierarchy {{role_depth}} levels deep and {{sharing_rules}} sharing rules. Its compliance team investigates data-access questions — "who could read this opportunity on 3 March, and why?" — and must answer for any date in the last {{audit_years}} years.
sections.problem: Design the data model that answers, for one org, "who could see record R at time T, at which level, and through which grants" and "which records of an object could user U see at time T". Cover: the entities (users and their role over time, the role tree, groups and nested membership, object defaults, sharing rules and their versions, manual shares, team memberships, record ownership history, and the field history criteria-based rules need), all with valid time; whether effective access is materialised as rows of (record, principal, level, reason) or computed at query time, and how materialised rows are kept right when the hierarchy, a group or a rule changes; how a point-in-time question is answered; and what is kept for {{audit_years}} years.
sections.constraints: An answer lists every grant path (default, ownership, hierarchy, a rule by id and version, a manual share, a team), not only yes or no. The model must never show a grant that did not exist at that time, and never omit one that did. Moving one user to another role must not rewrite the access rows of the whole org. Record field values enter the access model only for the fields a criteria-based rule references, and only as history of those fields.
sections.assumptions: Record counts, depths, rule counts and retention are hypothetical, and so are the access rules above. Times are UTC. Users can be deactivated; a deactivated user keeps their history. Implicit access between related records (for example, a child record granting read access to its parent) is out of scope unless a follow-up brings it in.
sections.criteria: Policy kept as temporal source data separate from derived access; valid-time role tree and nested groups (closure or equivalent) so membership is resolved as of T; ownership and criteria-field history kept minimally; grants carry a reason (rule id and version, share, team, hierarchy); a clear choice between materialised and computed access with a recalculation strategy that is incremental and whose in-progress state is visible; point-in-time queries defined; retention matched to {{audit_years}} years; cross-org analytics restricted to metadata; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does the role hierarchy apply to every object?
clarifications.a: In this exercise a flag per object says whether access is granted through the hierarchy. It is on for accounts and opportunities and off for one custom object.

clarifications.q: Can a sharing rule reduce access below the default?
clarifications.a: No. The default is the floor; everything else only widens it.

clarifications.q: If a group contains "role and subordinates", does its membership change when the hierarchy changes?
clarifications.a: Yes. Membership is resolved through the role tree in force at the time, so a reorg changes who is in the group without anyone editing it.

clarifications.q: What happens to manual shares when a record changes owner?
clarifications.a: In this exercise they are removed. Record that as an event with a time; do not just delete the rows.

clarifications.q: Is "could see" read or edit?
clarifications.a: Both. Report the highest level and every path that grants any level.

hints: Separate the policy (defaults, users' roles, the role tree, groups, rules, manual shares, teams, ownership — each with valid-from and valid-to) from derived effective access. The policy history is the source of truth; derived access is a cache you can rebuild for any time.

Access to a record at time T is a function of: its owner at T, the owner's role at T, the role tree at T, group membership at T, the rules in force at T and whether the record matched their criteria at T, and the manual shares and team memberships active at T.
A closure table (ancestor, descendant, depth) with valid time, for the role tree and for nested groups, turns hierarchy questions into joins.
followups: Walk one opportunity through a day: its owner's role is moved under a different manager at 10:00; at 14:00 a criteria-based rule starts sharing Closed Won opportunities with a Finance group; at 16:00 the opportunity is closed won. Who could see it at 09:00, 12:00 and 17:00, and through which grants?

A role near the top of a {{role_depth}}-level tree moves to another branch. Which derived rows change, how many in the worst case with {{org_records}} records, and what does a query see while they are being rewritten?
How do you store the role tree and nested groups over time so that "every role above role X at time T" and "every member of group G at time T" are single queries?
A criteria-based rule references two fields. What history of those fields must you keep, for how long, and how do you avoid copying record contents into the access store?
Product wants, across all orgs, "how many orgs use criteria-based rules, and how deep are their role trees". What may that pipeline read, and what must it never read?

rules.ask: A reorg moves 3,000 users to new roles. How many derived rows change, how long does recalculation take, and what does an auditor see for times inside that window?
The role tree changed twice on the day asked about. Which version of the tree does your recursion walk, and how do you make it the one in force at time T?
The auditor asks about a date eight months ago, before a sharing rule was deleted. Where does your model still know that the rule existed and whom it granted?
Compliance needs to know why the user could see the record, not only that they could. Which grant paths do you keep, and at which grain?
A subtree of 200 roles moves under a new parent. How many closure rows close and open, and how do you keep the old ones for point-in-time questions?

incidents: A reorg moved a top-level role in an org with {{org_records}} records. Recalculating derived access ran for hours; during that window the derived rows said some managers could not see their own team's records, and an access report generated inside the window was sent to the customer.

An administrator deleted a sharing rule and recreated it with the same name the next day. The access answer for the day in between showed grants through "the same" rule, because derived grants were keyed by rule name instead of rule id and version.
An investigation asks who could read a record {{audit_years}} years ago, but group membership history had been kept for only 90 days, so every grant through a group from that time is unknown.

templates.title: Custom objects and fields per org — schema metadata as data, analytics across different schemas
templates.subtopic: per-tenant schema metadata, stable field identity, schema evolution, metadata-only analytics

sections.scenario: A multi-tenant CRM lets each org define its own custom objects and custom fields — text, number, currency, date, picklist (with its list of values), lookup to another object, and formula. Administrators rename labels, convert some field types, add and deactivate picklist values, and delete fields; in this exercise's rule a deleted field can be restored for 15 days, after which it and its data are purged, and an object can have at most {{field_limit}} custom fields. About {{orgs}} orgs, averaging {{custom_fields_per_org}} custom fields each, make {{schema_changes_per_day}} schema changes a day. Two consumers depend on this metadata. Each customer can export its own records into its own analytical tables, which must follow its schema as it changes. The platform's product teams analyse metadata across orgs (field counts against the limit, field types in use, how often fields are deleted soon after creation) and must never read record contents; in this scenario labels, descriptions and picklist values are also customer data.
sections.problem: Design three things. (a) The metadata store: objects, fields, picklist values and relationships, each with a stable identity and a versioned history, so "what did org X's schema look like at time T" is a query. (b) How one org's records land in its own analytical tables when its schema changes (add, rename, type conversion, delete, restore, purge), and how one pipeline serves thousands of different schemas: per-org physical tables, a wide table with typed generic slots, attribute-value rows, or a semi-structured column — choose one and defend it. (c) Cross-org metadata analytics that answer "share of orgs with an object within 10% of the {{field_limit}} field limit", "field types in use" and "fields deleted within 30 days of creation", using no labels, values or record contents.
sections.constraints: A field keeps one stable id through renames; its API name is unique within its object at a point in time and can be reused after deletion. A purged field's data is removed from every copy, including the customer's export tables, within an agreed time that you state. Cross-org analytics read ids, types, counts and timestamps only. Schema history is immutable.
sections.assumptions: Org counts, field counts, change rates, the field limit and the 15-day restore window are hypothetical; so are the allowed type conversions (text to picklist, number to currency, picklist to text). Formula values are computed when read; an export may store them, labelled as computed at export time.
sections.criteria: Immutable ids for objects, fields and picklist values with versioned names, labels and types; schema-as-of-T as a query; a defended choice of physical layout for exports with its cost for wide reports and type changes; a field-id-to-column mapping so renames and API-name reuse are safe; delete, restore and purge as events with purge propagated and verified across copies; cross-org analytics on ids, types and counts only, with labels and values treated as customer data and small groups suppressed; incremental processing for bursts; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the API name a good key?
clarifications.a: No. It is unique only at a point in time: a deleted field's API name can be reused by a new field of another type.

clarifications.q: Do customers see the cross-org analytics?
clarifications.a: No. They are for the platform's product teams. A customer sees analytics about its own org.

clarifications.q: What does restoring a deleted field bring back?
clarifications.a: The field's definition and its data as they were at deletion, in this exercise's rule.

clarifications.q: Why are labels treated as customer data?
clarifications.a: Labels and picklist values can contain client names, project code names or health terms. Treat them like record contents.

clarifications.q: How often does a typical org change its schema?
clarifications.a: Most rarely; a few large orgs deploy hundreds of changes at once. Plan for bursts.

hints: Give every object, field and picklist value an immutable id; API names, labels, types and the deleted state are versioned attributes of that id.
Store schema history as valid-time versions per field (plus the change events that produced them), so the schema at time T is a filter rather than a replay of logs.
For the export, keep a per-org mapping from field id to warehouse column; a rename changes the mapping's label, never the data's location.
followups: An administrator renames the field with API name Region__c to Territory__c, then creates a new Region__c as a picklist. Show the metadata rows and the customer's analytical table afterwards.
A field is converted from text to picklist. What happens to its history in the export, and to a saved report that grouped by the old free-text values?
A field is deleted, restored 10 days later, deleted again and purged. Walk the metadata store, the export and the cross-org analytics through each step.
Compute "share of orgs with an object within 10% of the {{field_limit}} limit" from your model: which tables, which grain, and how does the result avoid identifying any org?
With {{orgs}} orgs and {{schema_changes_per_day}} changes a day, how do you avoid reprocessing a whole org on each change, and how do you prove that a purge reached every copy?

rules.ask: A customer's analyst wants 40 custom fields as columns over 30 million records. What does pivoting your attribute-value rows cost, and where do you materialise the wide shape?
A field converts from text to number. What happens to the values already stored as text, and to the queries that cast them?
A deleted field's API name is reused by a new field of a different type. How does your pipeline tell the two apart, in metadata and in the export?
Product asks for the 100 most common custom field labels across all orgs. What do you answer, and what could a label reveal about a customer?
{{orgs}} orgs, each with its own tables, and {{schema_changes_per_day}} changes a day: what does migration cost, and how do you convert the type of a column with years of history?

incidents: A large org's deployment deleted and re-created 300 fields with the same API names. The export pipeline, keyed on API names, attached years of history to the new fields, and the customer's dashboards changed overnight.

A purge completed in the primary store, but copies of the field's data remained in the customer's export tables and in a cross-org staging table that had captured picklist values "to compute type statistics".

A product dashboard of orgs near the {{field_limit}} field limit listed org ids with their largest custom objects' labels, and it was shared with a partner team that was not allowed to see customer data.

templates.title: Sandboxes and deployments — what changed in an org, when, by whom, and how to undo it
templates.subtopic: environment state as component-version intervals, deployments, drift, reversing deployments

sections.scenario: Each production org of a multi-tenant CRM can have sandboxes: copies of its metadata (and, for some sandbox types, data) where teams build and test changes. A change is built in a developer sandbox, promoted to an integration sandbox, then deployed to production. A deployment carries a set of metadata components (objects, fields, automation flows, code classes, page layouts, permission sets), can first be validated (checks and tests run, nothing changes), and in this exercise's rule is all-or-nothing. Administrators also change production directly through setup screens, which a setup audit trail records. Refreshing a sandbox replaces it with a fresh copy of production and discards the work in it; in this exercise a sandbox can be refreshed at most once every {{refresh_days}} days. There are {{orgs}} production orgs with about {{sandboxes_per_org}} sandboxes each, and {{deployments_per_day}} deployments a day across them. Customers want a change history per org; the platform wants deployment health analytics (success rates, test time, failures by component type) without reading customer code or record data.
sections.problem: Design the data model: environments (production orgs and sandboxes with their source, type, creation and refresh times); metadata components with a stable identity and versions identified by a content hash; the state of each environment over time (which version of each component was in force when); deployments (source, target, components and versions, validation runs, test results, status, who) and destructive changes; direct changes from the audit trail; and drift (production components that differ from what the last deployment put there). Answer: "what changed in production between Tuesday 09:00 and Thursday 18:00, by whom and how", "which deployment introduced this version of this flow", "which components is sandbox S behind production on", and "roll back deployment X" — and define rollback when nothing can be undone in place.
sections.constraints: Deployments are all-or-nothing. History is immutable: a refresh, a rollback or a failed deployment adds records, it never edits old ones. Component content is identified by hash; the platform's analytics see component types, counts, durations and outcomes, never the content of customer code, formulas or records. A sandbox's history before a refresh stays queryable for at least 90 days.
sections.assumptions: Counts, rates and the refresh interval are hypothetical, as are the deployment rules above. The audit trail records who, when, the kind of change and the component, but not always the full before and after content. Times are UTC.
sections.criteria: Environments with lineage and refresh events; components with stable ids and hashed versions; environment state as valid-time intervals tagged with the change that opened them; deployments with validations, test results and outcome-based status; direct changes from the audit trail in the same history; drift defined and detectable before a deployment; rollback as a reversing deployment with data consequences called out; immutable history including refreshes; health analytics on types, counts and durations only; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a deployment partly succeed?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. If one component or a required test fails, nothing changes in the target.

clarifications.q: Is a validation a deployment?
clarifications.a: It runs the same checks and tests but changes nothing. A later quick deploy can reuse a recent successful validation, in this exercise's rule.

clarifications.q: Does a deployment delete components?
clarifications.a: Only components it lists as destructive changes.

clarifications.q: How do we see direct changes in production?
clarifications.a: Through the setup audit trail: who, when, what kind of change and which component; the new version's hash comes from a metadata read after the change.

clarifications.q: What happens to a sandbox's history on refresh?
clarifications.a: Its content is replaced by a copy of production. What history your model keeps is your decision.

hints: Model environment state as intervals: (environment, component, version hash, valid_from, valid_to, change kind deployment|direct|refresh|creation, change id).
A rollback is a new deployment of the previous versions plus destructive changes for components the original added; record which deployment it reverses.
Drift is a production interval opened by a direct change after the last deployment of that component; a deployment that would overwrite it can be detected before it runs.
followups: Write the query shape for "what changed in production between two times": which table, which predicates on valid_from and valid_to, and how direct changes and deployments are labelled.
Deployment X added a field and changed a flow. Roll it back: which components and versions go into the reversing deployment, and what happens to values already written into the new field?
A developer sandbox was refreshed while a change was in progress. What does your model show about the work lost, and how would you warn before the refresh?
An administrator hotfixed a validation rule in production; a week later a deployment from the integration sandbox silently reverted it. Show how your model detects this before the deployment runs.
Deployment health across {{orgs}} orgs: define success rate and test duration per component type, and give the grain, partitioning and retention at {{deployments_per_day}} deployments a day.

rules.ask: Production also changes through setup screens that never touch the repository. How does your model see those changes, and which version wins on the next deployment?
The deployment you are reversing added a field that has since received 2 million values. What does your reversing deployment do to them, and who must approve it?
An administrator changes a flow at 10:00 and back at 15:00. Does your snapshot ever see the change, and can you say who made it?
Comparing a sandbox with production across 100,000 components: which keys and hashes make it cheap, and what about components that differ only in the order of their elements?
After a refresh, a pending deployment from that sandbox references component versions that no longer exist there. How does your model record that?

incidents: Automation refreshed an integration sandbox two days before a release. The work since the previous refresh is gone, the team cannot refresh again for {{refresh_days}} days, and it needs to know exactly which components and versions were lost.

A deployment that failed its tests was recorded as deployed because the status was taken from the request, not the outcome. The org's change history now shows component versions that never reached production.

A direct hotfix in production was overwritten by the next deployment. The customer asks which deployments, across their production org and its {{sandboxes_per_org}} sandboxes, have overwritten direct changes in the last quarter.

templates.title: Accounts, contacts and hierarchies — relationships, merges and rollups that keep their history
templates.subtopic: temporal hierarchies, many-to-many relationships, merge lineage, as-reported versus restated rollups

sections.scenario: In one customer org of a CRM, accounts (companies) form hierarchies through a parent account field: subsidiaries and regional offices under a global parent, up to {{max_depth}} levels deep in this org. A contact (a person) has one primary account and, in this exercise's rule, can be related to other accounts as well, with a role and start and end dates — a consultant working with several clients, a board member — which is true of about {{multi_account_share}} of contacts. Duplicate accounts and contacts are merged: one record survives, the losing records' related records (contacts, opportunities, cases, activities) move to the survivor, and the losers are deleted. In this exercise a merge cannot be undone, and deleted records can be restored for 15 days. The org has about {{accounts}} accounts and runs {{merges_per_month}} merges a month. Sales leadership reports pipeline rolled up to each global parent; account managers need a contact's history across accounts; data stewards must explain why last quarter's number for a parent changed.
sections.problem: Design the model in the org's analytical store, fed by the CRM's change events: accounts with their hierarchy over time; the account-contact relationships (primary and additional) over time; merges with lineage (loser, survivor, time, which related records moved); and the rollup of opportunity amounts to the global parent. Answer: "pipeline by global parent as of last quarter's end, as reported then", "the same, restated for merges and hierarchy changes since", "every account a contact has been related to, and when", and "which records did merge M move".
sections.constraints: The hierarchy has no cycles and is at most {{max_depth}} levels deep. A reference to a merged record resolves to its survivor, through chains of merges. Both "as reported" and "restated" views are available and labelled. Relationship history is never overwritten.
