Restated views change only through merges and dated hierarchy changes, never through silent edits.
sections.assumptions: Counts, shares, rates and the depth are hypothetical, as are the merge and restore rules above. Opportunity amounts are in one currency for this exercise. The change events carry record ids, the changed fields and a timestamp; a merge emits one event with the losing and surviving ids.
sections.criteria: Parent links with valid time and a derived closure or path per version; acyclicity and depth enforced at ingestion; a contact-account bridge with roles and dated intervals that distinguishes ending from deleting and restoring; a transitive merge map with lineage of moved records; facts keep their original keys; as-reported and restated rollups both defined, built from the same history and labelled; backdated changes visible; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does the losing record's id survive anywhere in the CRM?
clarifications.a: No. The merge event names the loser and the survivor; afterwards the loser's id no longer exists in the CRM. Your store must keep the mapping.

clarifications.q: Can an account change parent?
clarifications.a: Yes, after an acquisition or a reorganisation. The change has an effective time and data stewards sometimes backdate it.

clarifications.q: Which global parent does an opportunity roll up to?
clarifications.a: The global parent of the opportunity's account, in the hierarchy in force at the time the report is about (as reported) or today (restated).

clarifications.q: Can a merge involve accounts in different hierarchies?
clarifications.a: Yes. The survivor keeps its own parent unless the steward chooses otherwise.

clarifications.q: Are additional relationships ended or deleted?
clarifications.a: Both happen. Your model must tell "ended on a date" from "deleted by mistake and restored".

hints: Keep the hierarchy as a parent-link history (account, parent, valid_from, valid_to) and derive a closure or path per version; the global parent as of T is then a lookup.
A merge map (loser, survivor, merged_at), resolved transitively, lets facts keep their original account id and be re-pointed at query time.
"As reported" joins facts to the hierarchy and ids as they were at the report date; "restated" re-points facts through the merge map and today's hierarchy. Build both from the same history.
followups: Account B (with three open opportunities) is merged into A, which sits under a different global parent. Show the merge map row and last quarter's pipeline for both parents, as reported and restated.
A is merged into B, and later B into C. How do facts that still carry A's id find C, and what prevents a cycle in the merge map?
A data steward backdates a parent change to the start of the quarter. Which reports change, which do not, and how is the change visible to someone reading them?
How do you store the hierarchy so that "all descendants of global parent P as of date D" is cheap at {{accounts}} accounts and depth up to {{max_depth}}?
A deleted contact relationship is restored within 15 days. What do your history rows look like, and does "every account a contact was related to" show the gap?

rules.ask: The rollup runs the recursion over {{accounts}} accounts for every report. How do you stop on a cycle, and when would you precompute a closure table instead?
An account with 5,000 descendants moves to a new parent. How many closure rows change, and how do you keep the old version for "as reported"?
After you re-point the facts to the survivor, the steward asks what last quarter's report said before the merge. Where does that answer come from?
A merged loser is deleted in the CRM. Is that the same kind of deletion as a mistaken delete that will be restored within 15 days? How does your model tell them apart?
What is the grain of your bridge, and how does it show a contact who left an account and came back a year later?

incidents: A bulk import created a cycle (A's parent is B and B's parent is A) in an org whose hierarchy is up to {{max_depth}} levels deep. The nightly rollup's recursion ran until the job timed out, and the pipeline dashboard kept showing yesterday's numbers labelled as today's.

A data-quality project ran {{merges_per_month}} merges in one weekend. Last quarter's pipeline per global parent changed in the restated view, and sales leadership compared it with a board deck built on the as-reported numbers, with neither labelled.
Opportunity facts that still carried a loser's account id were dropped by an inner join to the current accounts table, and revenue for merged accounts vanished from the dashboard.

templates.title: API allocation use — org-days that crossed 80% and 100% of a licence-based allocation
templates.subtopic: as-of joins to two histories, capped formulas, running totals per day, re-loaded feeds

sections.scenario: A multi-tenant CRM gives each org a daily allocation of API requests that grows with its licences. In this exercise's rule (check current docs for the product's own rule, which may use a rolling 24 hours), the allocation is fixed for each UTC calendar day: LEAST(base_requests + per_licence × licences, max_requests) from the org's edition, plus the extra_requests of every add-on active that day. Requests are counted into hourly buckets in api_usage (counts only; nothing about a request's content). The platform's usage team warns an org's administrators when it reaches 80% and 100% of its allocation, and wants a daily report of the org-days that crossed those thresholds, and when.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns org_id, usage_day, allocation, requests, pct_used, crossed_80_at, crossed_100_at: one row per org and UTC day (the sample covers {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}) whose requests, the day's total, is at least 80% of that day's allocation, ordered by usage_day, org_id. The edition and the licence count used for a day are the ones in force at the start of the day (00:00 UTC): in each history, the latest row for the org with effective_at at or before that instant. An add-on is active on a day when starts_on <= day <= ends_on. pct_used is ROUND(100.0 * requests / allocation, 1). crossed_80_at is the hour_start of the first bucket at which the day's running total reached 80% of the allocation; crossed_100_at is the same for 100%, or NULL if the day never reached it. {{feed_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Thresholds are inclusive: a day at exactly 80% has crossed. Compare integers (requests * 100 >= allocation * 80), not rounded percentages. The sample has {{orgs}} orgs and {{usage_rows}} usage rows; production has hundreds of thousands of orgs and years of hourly buckets.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical editions, licence counts, add-ons and request counts; the formula is this exercise's rule, not a product's. Every org has an edition row and a licence row before the first day. Days are UTC calendar days and hour_start is always on the hour.
sections.criteria: Allocation per org-day from both histories as of 00:00 (inclusive), the cap on the licence part only, add-ons summed per day with inclusive dates; a running total partitioned by org and day; inclusive integer threshold comparisons; NULL for an uncrossed 100%; at the hardest level, the latest load per hour; deterministic ordering; can explain rolling windows, streaming warnings and late corrections.

clarifications.q: Licences were added at 14:00. Does that raise the same day's allocation?
clarifications.a: No. The allocation is fixed at 00:00 UTC; the change counts from the next day.

clarifications.q: And a change effective at exactly 00:00?
clarifications.a: It applies to that day: effective at or before the start of the day.

clarifications.q: Does the cap apply to add-ons?
clarifications.a: No. The cap limits the licence-based part; add-ons are added on top of it.

clarifications.q: Should days below 80%, or days with no usage, appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only org-days at or above 80%.

clarifications.q: One bucket takes the day from 70% to 110%. What are the crossing times?
clarifications.a: Both crossed_80_at and crossed_100_at are that bucket's hour_start.

hints: Compute the allocation per (org_id, day) first. A LATERAL subquery with ORDER BY effective_at DESC LIMIT 1 picks the row in force at 00:00; do it for editions and for licences.
The running total is SUM(requests) OVER (PARTITION BY org_id, day ORDER BY hour_start); the first crossing is MIN(hour_start) FILTER (WHERE running * 100 >= allocation * 80).
Sum the add-ons per org and day before combining them with anything hourly; joining add-ons to hourly rows multiplies the requests.
followups: Suppose the allocation applied to a rolling 24 hours instead of a calendar day. Rewrite the crossing test over hourly buckets. Which allocation is "in force" for a window that spans a licence change?
Warnings must go out within minutes of crossing, not in a daily report. What state does a streaming job keep per org, and how do you prove it agrees with this query afterwards?
A late re-load lowers an hour's count after an 80% warning has already gone out. Is the warning retracted, and what does this report show?
An org's licences fell mid-month. Write the follow-on query that lists orgs whose last seven days of usage would have crossed 100% under the allocation in force today.

rules.ask: An org has two add-ons active on the same day. How many rows does each hourly bucket produce after your join, and what happens to SUM(requests)?
For a day three days ago, which licence count does your query use: the one in force at 00:00 that day, or today's?
You compare a rounded percentage with 80. Which day can that misclassify, and why is requests * 100 >= allocation * 80 exact?
Does your running total restart at midnight, or does yesterday's usage push today's crossing earlier? Show the PARTITION BY.
An hour was loaded three times. Which load does your query keep, and why is adding the loads wrong?

incidents: An org added licences at 15:00 UTC and its integration reached 100% at 19:00. Support had told the customer the higher allocation applied immediately; this report, which applies licence changes from the next day, flagged the org, and the customer escalated over a warning they believed was wrong.
A version of this report that summed every load of a re-loaded hour counted late usage twice and sent 100% warnings to orgs that were nowhere near their allocation.

templates.title: Unified customer profiles with identity resolution, unmerges and consent
templates.subtopic: match rules, merge graphs, unmerge, consent propagation

sections.scenario: A customer data platform lets each customer org bring together what it knows about the same person from {{sources}} sources: CRM contacts and leads, an online store's accounts, a loyalty programme, support cases, event registrations and email subscriber lists. The largest org holds {{records}} source records. Each org configures its own match rules (for example "same normalised email" or "same last name and same normalised postal address"), and the platform builds one unified profile per person, which marketing segments, service consoles and analytics all read. Consent is recorded per purpose ({{purposes}} purposes in the largest org, such as email marketing, SMS and analytics) and arrives from several of the sources, sometimes in conflict.
sections.problem: Design identity resolution and the unified profile. Cover how source records are normalised and matched; how matches become profiles and how a profile id stays stable as records arrive, change and are deleted; how an org changes its match rules without taking its profiles offline; how a wrong merge is undone (an unmerge) and what happens downstream; how consent is carried with the profile, including conflicts between sources; how a person's deletion request is honoured everywhere; and how the system explains to an org administrator why two records were merged.
sections.constraints: A new or changed source record reaches the unified profile within 15 minutes. A consent withdrawal must stop all activation for that purpose within {{withdraw_minutes}} minutes, whichever source it arrives from. Matching never crosses orgs. Downstream segments refer to profile ids, so ids must not churn without reason. A deletion request is completed across every store, including derived ones, within the window the org's policy sets.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings and counts are hypothetical. Match-rule behaviour, consent precedence and deletion windows are this exercise's rules; check current docs for any real product's behaviour. Sources deliver either change events or periodic full extracts.
sections.criteria: Normalisation before matching, with per-rule blocking keys; a persistent match graph with edges labelled by rule, and profiles derived from it; stable profile ids with a clear survivorship rule on merge and on split; detection of over-connected values (frequency caps, blocklists, cluster-size alarms) before they merge; rule changes re-resolved in a shadow version and cut over with a diff, not in place; unmerge and "never merge" constraints that survive reruns, with downstream retraction; consent as a separate, per-purpose stream with precedence rules and enforcement at activation time; deletion propagated to derived stores and exports with proof; per-org isolation; adapts to each incident with containment, repair and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are match rules deterministic or probabilistic?
clarifications.a: Deterministic rules configured by the org. You may propose a scored fuzzy rule as an extension, but say how an administrator would understand and override it.

clarifications.q: Is matching transitive? If A matches B and B matches C, is A the same person as C?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes by default. Tell me what that costs you.

clarifications.q: When sources disagree on consent, which wins?
clarifications.a: The org sets a policy; the default in this exercise is the most recent explicit choice per purpose, with withdrawal never overridden by an older grant.

clarifications.q: Do downstream systems hold copies of profiles?
clarifications.a: Yes: segment exports to email and advertising tools, and cached profiles in the service console.

clarifications.q: Can an administrator force two records apart permanently?
clarifications.a: Yes. A "never merge" pair must survive every later rule run.

hints: Separate the match graph (records as nodes, rule matches as edges, each edge with the rule that produced it) from the profile built on top of it. Unmerges and explanations are much easier when the edges are kept.

Some values (a shared support mailbox, a call-centre phone number, a household email) connect thousands of unrelated people. Decide how a rule recognises a value that is too common to identify anyone.
Treat consent as its own event stream keyed by person and purpose, evaluated at activation time, not only copied into a nightly profile.
followups: Walk through one new loyalty-programme record that matches two existing profiles. What changes, and which profile id survives?
An org adds a rule that matches on phone number. How do you re-resolve {{records}} records without disrupting segments that are running today?
A source record that was the only link between two halves of a profile is deleted. What happens to the profile id, its segments and its consent?
A consent withdrawal arrives from the email tool while a segment export to an advertising audience is in flight. How do you meet the {{withdraw_minutes}}-minute bound?
How would you measure over-merging and under-merging per org without reading record contents across orgs?

rules.ask: One shared mailbox links 40,000 records into one component. How does your design notice, and what do the 40,000 people's profiles look like afterwards?
An org administrator asks why two of their customers were merged. What exactly does your system show them, and how do they undo it?
The loyalty programme's address is newer but the CRM's address was verified by a person. Which survives into the profile, and who decides?
A customer withdraws email consent at 09:00 and your next batch runs tonight. What reaches them in between?
The deleted record had already been copied into three segment exports and a cached service-console profile. How do you know every copy is gone?

incidents: An org adds a phone-number rule. Within an hour, 30,000 contacts who all list the same call-centre number collapse into one profile, and a scheduled campaign sends one person's offer to the email address that profile happened to keep.

An email tool, one of the {{sources}} sources, re-sends its full extract after its own upgrade with every address lowercased and trimmed. The platform treats them as new values, and the largest org's profile count jumps by 12% overnight.

A consent withdrawal recorded in the service console is not applied for 9 hours because that source's change events were stuck behind a full re-resolution; the person receives two SMS messages after opting out, far outside the {{withdraw_minutes}}-minute bound.

templates.title: Sandbox refresh with consistent masking of personal data
templates.subtopic: production copies, deterministic masking, referential integrity

sections.scenario: Customer orgs develop and test changes in sandboxes: copies of their production org's configuration and, for some sandbox types, its data. A large org has {{data_size}} of record data across {{objects}} standard and custom objects, and {{sandboxes}} sandboxes that its developers, testers and outside implementation partners refresh from production on their own schedules. Production holds personal data about the org's customers: names, emails, phone numbers, postal addresses, dates of birth, free-text notes and attached files. The platform is adding masked refreshes: personal data is replaced with realistic but fictitious values during the copy, so testers can work with production-shaped data without seeing anyone's real details.
sections.problem: Design the masked sandbox refresh. Cover how the copy is taken without hurting production; how fields are classified as personal (and what happens to a field nobody classified); how values are masked so that the same real value always becomes the same masked value within a sandbox (so duplicate rules, joins and matching still behave); how formats, uniqueness and relationships between records are preserved; how free text and files are handled; how partial copies (a sample of records) keep related records together; and how you prove that no unmasked personal value ever reached the sandbox.
sections.constraints: A full refresh finishes within {{window_hours}} hours. Unmasked personal data must never be written to sandbox storage, logs, temporary files or search indexes, not even briefly. Masking must be repeatable within a sandbox and different between sandboxes, so values cannot be correlated across them. Production users must not notice a refresh. Automations in a sandbox must never reach a real person.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, timings and counts are hypothetical. Sandbox types, which ones carry data and how refreshes are scheduled are this exercise's rules; check current docs. Field metadata can carry a data-classification label set by the org's administrators, but many fields have none.
sections.criteria: Copy from a consistent snapshot or replica with throttling, never from the live write path; masking inside the pipeline before any sandbox write, with no unmasked spill to logs or temporary storage; classification from labels plus detection, failing closed on unlabelled personal-looking fields; keyed deterministic masking per sandbox that is consistent across objects and copies, preserves formats, keeps unique fields unique (collision handling) and is not correlatable between sandboxes; secret lifecycle tied to the sandbox, with rotation forcing a full re-mask; free text redacted or replaced and files excluded or replaced by placeholders; partial copies with referential closure and size bounds; outbound email, SMS and integration endpoints disabled or redirected in sandboxes; an audit trail and sampling checks proving no real values were copied; adapts to each incident.

clarifications.q: Can the masked values be random?
clarifications.a: They must be consistent: the same real email masks to the same fake email everywhere in that sandbox, including in lookups and in other objects that store a copy of it.

clarifications.q: Who decides which fields are personal?
clarifications.a: The org's administrators label fields; the platform may suggest labels. You decide what happens to unlabelled fields.

clarifications.q: Do tests need valid formats?
clarifications.a: Yes. Validation rules and integrations in the sandbox expect well-formed emails, phone numbers and postcodes, and unique fields must stay unique.

clarifications.q: Are attached files copied?
clarifications.a: For full copies, today they are. Decide what masked refreshes do with them.

clarifications.q: Can a refresh be partial?
clarifications.a: Yes: a template of objects and a sample size per object. Related records must come along so the sample is usable.

hints: Mask in the copy pipeline, between reading production and writing the sandbox. Copying first and masking afterwards leaves real data in the sandbox for hours.

A keyed, deterministic transformation (for example an HMAC of the normalised value with a per-sandbox secret, used to pick a fake value from a dictionary or to format-preserve) gives consistency within a sandbox and no correlation across sandboxes.
Fail closed: a field that looks personal but has no label should be masked or blanked, and reported, not copied.
followups: Walk through one contact record and its related account, cases and email messages. Which values are masked, by what rule, and how do the relationships survive?
A unique field (an external customer number) must stay unique after masking. How do you guarantee it?
Free-text case descriptions mention customers by name and phone number. What do you do with them, and what does a tester lose?
An org's partial refresh samples 1% of accounts. How do you choose the related records so the sample is consistent, and how do you bound its size?
Auditors ask you to prove no real personal value reached any of the {{sandboxes}} sandboxes last quarter. What evidence does your design produce?

rules.ask: Encrypted values are consistent and reversible. Who holds the key, and what happens if a tester's sandbox and that key end up in the same place?
Hashing an email without a secret means anyone can hash a known address and look for it. How do you prevent that, and how do you keep the email format valid?
The same customer appears in contacts, in a case's supplied email and in an email message. With random values, do those still line up in the sandbox?
For the hours between the copy and the masking job, real data sits in a sandbox that contractors can reach. How do you justify that?
Your detector misses a phone number written as words in a note. What is the second line of defence?

incidents: A custom field added to cases last month holds customers' mobile numbers, but nobody labelled it. After a refresh, an SMS automation in one of the {{sandboxes}} sandboxes sends test messages to 2,000 real customers.

A refresh of {{data_size}} overruns its {{window_hours}}-hour window by a day because one object with millions of attached files is copied and scanned file by file; testers start work against a half-loaded sandbox.

The masking secret for a sandbox is rotated between a full refresh and a later partial top-up. Contacts copied before and after no longer mask to the same values, duplicate rules fire on every new record, and test matches fail.

templates.title: Org usage analytics for many thousands of orgs, without reading record contents
templates.subtopic: multi-tenant usage analytics, adoption, limit consumption, data minimisation

sections.scenario: The platform hosts {{orgs}} customer orgs. Product teams want to know which of {{features}} features are adopted, by how many orgs and users, and how adoption changes after a release. Each org's administrators want to see their own org's logins, active users, feature use and how much of each limit (API calls, data storage, asynchronous jobs) they have consumed, and they want an alert before they hit one. Telemetry runs to {{events}} events a day. Org data is the customer's: usage analytics may use metadata about activity, never the contents of records.
sections.problem: Design the usage analytics system end to end. Cover what events are emitted and with which fields (and how you keep record contents out); collection and deduplication; the models for logins, feature adoption and limit consumption; the views for an org's own administrators versus product teams looking across orgs; near-real-time limit consumption with alerts at thresholds; and how one very large org or one misbehaving integration does not distort everything else.
sections.constraints: A limit alert fires within {{alert_minutes}} minutes of consumption crossing a threshold. An org administrator sees only their own org; product teams see aggregates across orgs, with user identities pseudonymised and small groups suppressed. No field values, record names, search terms or free text may enter the analytics store. Events can arrive hours late when a region's collectors back up. The cost of the system should grow roughly with event volume, not with the number of orgs times the number of features.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts, limits and thresholds are hypothetical, as is how limits are allocated; check current docs. Every event carries an org id, a pseudonymous user id, a timestamp and an event type.
sections.criteria: An event schema allowlist enforced at collection, with dropped-field reporting and scanning for content that slipped through, plus a purge path; separation of the exact, low-latency limit counter from the analytical adoption path; idempotent ingestion keyed by event id, event-time windows with late-data correction and completeness signals; adoption metrics defined precisely, with integration users separated from people; per-org isolation in the administrator view and pseudonymised, suppressed aggregates across orgs; skew handling for the largest orgs; exact distinct counts where an org sees them and sketches where they are mergeable aggregates; alert freshness monitored as its own signal; adapts to each incident with containment, repair and prevention.

clarifications.q: What counts as adopting a feature?
clarifications.a: Define it. A sensible default: an org with at least one active user of the feature in a rolling 28 days; for users, at least one use in the period.

clarifications.q: Can product teams see which orgs use a feature?
clarifications.a: Named orgs only for teams that manage those customers' accounts and with a purpose; everyone else sees aggregates.

clarifications.q: Do administrators see individual users?
clarifications.a: Their own users, yes, by name, inside their own org's view. Cross-org views never show a person.

clarifications.q: Are integration users counted as active users?
clarifications.a: Not as people. Logins by integration users must be distinguishable.

clarifications.q: How exact must limit consumption be?
clarifications.a: The alert must not be late; the daily statement must be exact.

hints: Make the event schema an allowlist enforced at the collector: unknown properties are dropped and reported, not stored.
Two different products share one event stream: an exact, fast counter path for limits, and an analytical path for adoption. They need different stores and different latencies.
Distinct users across orgs and days do not add up; plan for exact distinct counts where an org sees them and sketches where product teams aggregate.
followups: Walk through one login event and one feature-use event from emission to the administrator's dashboard and to the product team's adoption report.
How do you compute weekly active users per feature across {{orgs}} orgs efficiently, and what is exact versus approximate?
An engineer adds a property to a feature event that turns out to contain search terms typed by users. How does your design stop it, or detect and purge it?
Events from one region arrive six hours late. What does the adoption report show in the meantime, and how is it corrected?
How would you show the effect of a release on adoption without misleading the team when the largest orgs adopt first?

rules.ask: Keeping every raw property "just in case" means record contents eventually land there. What stops that, and who is accountable for it?
An org administrator sees 1,003 active users while their licence count says 1,000. What do you show them, and why?
One org produces 8% of all events. What happens to the partition it lands on, and to the jobs that read it?
Your streaming counter crashes and restarts from a checkpoint. How do you avoid double counting API calls toward an org's limit?
A product manager filters adoption by country and industry until a cell holds two orgs. What does your system return?

incidents: A release adds a property to a feature event that carries the text users typed into a search box. For two days customer names and email addresses flow into the analytics store before anyone notices.

One org's misconfigured integration logs in and fails 40,000 times an hour; that org's active-user count, the login-failure dashboard and several adoption ratios across all {{orgs}} orgs are distorted for a week.

The counter path behind limit alerts lags by two hours during a regional backlog. Several orgs hit their API allocation without the promised alert {{alert_minutes}} minutes earlier, and their integrations start failing.

templates.title: Fair asynchronous job processing across tenants on shared workers
templates.subtopic: per-org queues, fair share, limits, noisy neighbours

sections.scenario: Customer orgs run asynchronous work on the platform: queued jobs from their own code, scheduled batch jobs that process records in chunks, automations that run after a record is saved, and bulk data loads. {{orgs}} orgs share a pool of {{workers}} workers in a region, and at peak they submit {{peak_jobs}} jobs a minute. Each org may run up to {{daily_limit}} asynchronous executions in a rolling 24 hours, and every execution runs under per-transaction limits on CPU time, queries and rows touched. A few orgs submit most of the work, and their jobs differ in length by three orders of magnitude.
sections.problem: Design the asynchronous job system. Cover how jobs are accepted (including the daily limit), queued and dispatched; what "fair" means between orgs and how the scheduler achieves it; how one org with a surge cannot delay everyone else; how long jobs and short jobs share workers; how a job is leased, retried and made safe to run twice; how jobs from the same org that touch the same records avoid fighting over locks; and what each org and the platform's operators can see about queue health.
sections.constraints: A small org's job should start within seconds even while large orgs have deep backlogs. No org should be starved, and an org's share should not depend on how many jobs it can enqueue. Workers can be lost at any time. Retries must not send an email twice or double-apply an update the job was written to make once. The daily limit is enforced at acceptance, and an org learns it is close before it is cut off.
sections.assumptions: All counts, limits and timings are hypothetical, as are the job types and their limits; check current docs for any real platform's rules. Jobs read and write the org's records in a shared relational store partitioned by org.
sections.criteria: Per-org (and per-class) queues with a scheduler that shares worker-seconds fairly (deficit round robin, weighted fair queuing or virtual-time scheduling) and an efficient structure to pick the next org; per-org concurrency caps and admission control with the rolling daily limit and early warning; urgency classes across orgs with org priorities only within an org; leases, heartbeats and fencing tokens; idempotency keys for side effects and at-least-once execution stated plainly; lock-contention handling by serialising jobs per record key or by backoff with jitter; retry budgets and poison-job quarantine; autoscaling that responds to aggregate demand rather than one org's surge; per-org queue age and worker-seconds as the operator's and the org's views; adapts to each incident.

clarifications.q: Should fair mean the same number of jobs per org?
clarifications.a: Define it. Jobs differ hugely in length, so say whether you share job starts, worker-seconds or something else, and whether larger customers get larger weights.

clarifications.q: Can an org mark jobs as urgent?
clarifications.a: Jobs started by a user waiting on screen are more urgent than scheduled batch work. Org-set priorities apply only within that org.

clarifications.q: How long can a job run?
clarifications.a: Each execution has a CPU-time limit; batch jobs are split into chunks that each run as one execution.

clarifications.q: What happens to a job when its worker dies?
clarifications.a: Decide. The platform may run a job again; your design must make that safe.

clarifications.q: Can the worker pool grow?
clarifications.a: Yes, within minutes, but not instantly and not without limit.

hints: A single global first-in-first-out queue gives the whole pool to whoever enqueues fastest. Queue per org (and per class), and let the scheduler choose which org's queue to take from next.
Measure fairness in worker-seconds consumed, not in jobs started: deficit round robin or weighted fair queuing over per-org queues, with per-org concurrency caps.
Leases with heartbeats and an expiry let another worker pick up a job whose worker died; an idempotency key per side effect makes the second run harmless.
followups: Walk through what happens when one org enqueues three million jobs at 09:00 while a thousand small orgs each enqueue a few.
How does the scheduler choose the next job to run? Give the data structure and its cost per dispatch with {{orgs}} orgs.
Two hundred jobs from one org all update the same parent record and fail on lock contention, then retry. What does your design do?
A worker pauses for 90 seconds in garbage collection, its lease expires, another worker starts the job, and then the first worker wakes up. What prevents a double write?
How would you set per-org weights and concurrency caps, and how would you show an org why its jobs are waiting?

rules.ask: One org enqueues three million jobs ahead of everyone. How long does a small org's single job now wait?
If every org marks its jobs high priority, what does your priority mean? Who is allowed to set it?
One org's jobs each run for 10 minutes and another's for 50 milliseconds. Is your round robin still fair?
The surge comes from one org. Do you add workers for it? Who pays, and does it fix the wait for others?
The job sends an email and then the worker dies before acknowledging. Show me how the retry knows not to send it again.

incidents: One org starts a data load that enqueues three million jobs at 09:00. Within twenty minutes, the p99 wait to start for every other org rises from 4 seconds to 40 minutes, and user-initiated jobs time out on screen.

A release introduces a job type that runs until its CPU-time limit and is retried five times. It ends up occupying a third of the {{workers}} workers while its org's backlog looks normal by job count.
A worker restart during peak loses its leases; 18,000 jobs run twice, and one org's customers receive duplicate order-confirmation emails.

templates.title: Archiving old records while keeping them queryable and reportable
templates.subtopic: archival tiers, related records, retention, legal holds, live-plus-archive reporting

sections.scenario: Orgs accumulate records they rarely touch: closed cases, completed tasks, old email messages and field-history rows. The largest org's case-related objects hold {{rows}} rows, and the primary store is slower and more expensive the more it holds. The platform is offering archiving to {{orgs}} orgs: each org sets a policy per object (for example "cases closed more than {{archive_months}} months ago"), archived records move out of the primary store, users can still find and open them, reports can still include them, and they are deleted for good when the org's retention period ({{retention_years}} years by default) ends, unless a legal hold applies.
sections.problem: Design archiving. Cover how records are selected under each org's policy; how a record moves together with its related records (comments, emails, attachments, history) without loss or duplication; where archived records live and in what format; how users find and open one, and how reports combine live and archived records; how record access rules still apply to archived records; how schema changes after archiving are handled; and how retention, legal holds, deletion requests and restores work.
sections.constraints: Archiving must not slow the org's daytime work. No record may be lost or exist in both stores as a live record. Opening one archived record by id takes under two seconds; a report over archived data may take minutes. A user who could not see a record before it was archived must not see it afterwards. A deletion request for a person must reach archived records too. Retention and legal holds are per org.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, ages and periods are hypothetical. Retention defaults, legal-hold behaviour and which objects can be archived are this exercise's rules; check current docs. The primary store supports transactions within an org; the archive store does not need to.
sections.criteria: Policy-driven selection per org and object with throttled, off-peak batches; families of related records archived together; copy, verify, delete with a durable batch manifest and idempotent reruns; a columnar archive partitioned by org, object and time, with a key-value index for opens and stubs or redirects for lookups from live records; access checks applied to archived records using stored owner and sharing-relevant fields evaluated against current rules; schema versions recorded with archived data and a union view with nulls or defaults for later fields; retention deletion as a scheduled, auditable job that checks legal holds at execution time with a grace period after policy changes; deletion requests that reach the archive; reconciliation counts per batch proving each record is in exactly one place; adapts to each incident.

clarifications.q: Can archived records be edited?
clarifications.a: No. They can be restored to the primary store, edited there, and archived again later.

clarifications.q: What about live records that look up an archived one, such as an open case whose parent case was archived?
clarifications.a: Decide. The lookup must not break for users.

clarifications.q: Do reports need to show live and archived records together?
clarifications.a: Yes, for a defined set of report types; it may be slower.

clarifications.q: Who can place a legal hold?
clarifications.a: The org's administrators, on records matching a filter (for example every case for one account). A hold overrides both archiving and retention deletion.

clarifications.q: Does sharing still matter for archived records?
clarifications.a: Yes. Access must be checked as it would be for the live record, under this exercise's sharing rules.

hints: Make a move a copy, then a verification, then a delete, with a durable manifest per batch, so a crash at any step is safe to rerun.
Choose the unit of archiving as a record and its whole family of related records, chosen by the parent's policy, so the archive never holds orphans and the primary never holds dangling children.
Archived data is cold and read in bulk: a columnar format partitioned by org, object and close month, plus a small key-value index by record id for single-record opens.
followups: Walk through archiving one closed case with 40 comments, 12 emails and 3 attachments. What is written where, in what order, and what happens if the process dies halfway?
How do you keep the access check correct for archived records when the role hierarchy and sharing rules change after archiving?
A field was added to cases after half of them were archived. How do reports that combine live and archived cases treat it?
An org shortens retention, and a day later places a legal hold on cases that the new retention period has started to delete. What does your design guarantee?
How do you prove to an org that every record selected for archiving in a month is in exactly one place?

rules.ask: The rows are still in the primary store with a flag. Which of the cost and speed problems has that solved?
A user opens one archived case by id. Which file holds it, and how do you find it in under two seconds?
The copy succeeds and the process dies before the delete. On rerun, what stops the archive holding the case twice?
A legal hold arrives for records whose expiry has already been scheduled. How does the hold win?
The live and archived halves have different columns and different access paths. How does one report query both and still apply sharing?

incidents: An archiving run for the largest org copies a batch of 2 million cases, crashes before deleting them from the primary store, and on restart copies them again. Reports combining live and archived cases double count that month.

A policy archives closed cases but its selection leaves their attachments behind. Six million attachments in the primary store now point at parents users cannot reach from them; they are still billed, still hold personal data, and the next deletion request for a customer misses them.
An org cuts retention from {{retention_years}} years to 2. Deletion starts that night; the next morning legal counsel places a hold on one account's cases, some of which have already been deleted.

templates.title: Writing a one-year technical strategy the team will actually follow
templates.subtopic: direction setting, trade-offs, buy-in, keeping a plan alive

platform: the pipelines that ingest customers' sources into the customer data platform
the org usage analytics that product teams and customer admins rely on
the telemetry pipeline behind automation run and fault reporting
pressure: the number of orgs on the platform is expected to double
two new regions must keep customer data inside their borders
a legacy store that half the pipelines depend on is being retired within the year
on-call load has risen every quarter for a year

sections.scenario: You are the most senior engineer on a team of {{team}} that owns {{platform}}. The year ahead is shaped by one fact: {{pressure}}. Your director asks you to write the team's technical strategy for the year. The last two strategy documents the team wrote were approved, presented once, and then ignored: within a quarter, work was being chosen ticket by ticket again.
sections.problem: How do you produce a strategy that changes what the team does? Cover how you find out where the system and the team really are; who you involve and when; what the document says and what it leaves out; how you make the trade-offs explicit (what the team will stop doing, not only start); how you get commitment from the team, your director and the teams that depend on you; and how you keep it alive through the year as things change. Then tell me about a real time you set technical direction for a team, and whether people followed it, or say you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Roadmap requests from other teams will keep arriving all year. You do not control headcount. The strategy must fit on a few pages.
sections.assumptions: The team, platform and pressures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Starts with a diagnosis grounded in evidence (incidents, on-call load, cost, data growth, dependencies, what customers and internal users report) and in the team's own view; a small number of guiding choices tied to the year's main pressure, with explicit trade-offs and things the team will stop or defer; involves the team early so they shape it, and engages the director and dependent teams on the rules for taking new work; concrete first actions and measurable signals; regular reviews with criteria for changing course; keeps it short and visible; real example with what changed in people's behaviour and the candidate's own role, or an honest hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Why were the earlier strategies ignored?
clarifications.a: Ask the team. The visible facts: they listed many goals with no order, nobody tracked them, and the first urgent request displaced them.

clarifications.q: Does the director expect a specific format?
clarifications.a: No. They expect something they can defend to their own leadership and that the team believes in.

clarifications.q: Can the strategy say no to other teams' requests?
clarifications.a: It can set rules for what the team takes on; the director must back those rules.

clarifications.q: How long do I have?
clarifications.a: About six weeks before the planning cycle closes.

hints: A strategy is a diagnosis, a few guiding choices and the actions that follow from them. A list of goals is not a strategy.
Saying what the team will not do, and how it will decide on new requests, is what keeps the plan alive when the first urgent request arrives.
Plan the review points (monthly or quarterly) and the signals that would tell you the strategy is wrong.
followups: What would you look at in the first two weeks to diagnose where {{platform}} really stands?
Name two things your strategy would explicitly stop or defer, and how you would explain that to the teams who wanted them.
Three months in, an urgent request from a large customer does not fit the strategy. What happens?
How would you know at the half-year mark whether the strategy is working, and what would make you change it?
In your real example, what did people do differently because of the direction you set, and what did you get wrong?

rules.ask: Goals say where you want to be. What are the two or three choices that say how you will get there, and what they rule out?
What did you expect to hear, and what would genuinely change your plan if you heard it?
Halfway through the first quarter, an estimate turns out double. Which part of your roadmap gives way first, and who decides?
One senior engineer on the team disagrees with your main choice and says so in the review. What do you do?
Which parts of the strategy came from other people, and how did they see their input in it?

templates.title: Introducing design reviews to a team that sees them as bureaucracy
templates.subtopic: introducing process, lightweight reviews, measuring whether it helps

incident: a new connector that read every record of a source on each run and exhausted several customers' API allocations
a change to how source records were matched that merged unrelated customers' profiles in one org
a schema change that silently dropped a field from the usage reports customer admins rely on
pace: ship weekly and are proud of it
have a release next month that leadership is watching
were previously on a team where reviews took weeks

sections.scenario: You lead a team of {{team}} engineers building ingestion connectors and transformations for a customer data platform used by many customer orgs. Last quarter, {{incident}}. The design behind it was never seen by anyone but its author; in the post-incident review, two engineers said they would have spotted the problem in ten minutes. You want the team to review designs before building significant changes. The team, who {{pace}}, see design reviews as bureaucracy that slows them down.
sections.problem: How do you introduce design reviews so that they catch problems like this without the team resenting them? Cover what you would change and what you would not; what counts as a change that needs a review; what a review looks like (who, how long, what document); how you get the team to adopt it rather than comply with it; how you know whether it is working; and what you would do if it is not. Then tell me about a real time you introduced or changed an engineering practice, and what happened, or say you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You can set team practices, but the team's speed is something your director values and watches. You cannot hire a review board.
sections.assumptions: The team, incident and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses what went wrong in the incident rather than blaming the author; introduces a narrow, explicit threshold and a cheap format (short template, asynchronous, a named reviewer, a deadline); involves the team in designing the practice and starts with willing engineers; reviews own designs first and accepts criticism visibly; measures outcomes the team cares about (incidents caught in review, rework avoided, time from design to ship) and adjusts or drops parts that do not help; handles a resistant high performer with curiosity and clear expectations; keeps the director informed with evidence; real example with what changed and what the candidate personally did, or an honest hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does every change need a review?
clarifications.a: You decide the threshold. Most changes in the last quarter were small.

clarifications.q: Does the team have any written designs today?
clarifications.a: A few engineers write short notes in the ticket; most do not.

clarifications.q: Who reviewed code?
clarifications.a: Code review is routine and quick; it is the designs that nobody saw.

clarifications.q: Will leadership support a short slowdown?
clarifications.a: If you can show it reduces incidents like the one last quarter.

hints: Make the threshold explicit and narrow: changes that touch customers' limits, data matching, schemas others read, or anything hard to undo.
Make it cheap: a one-page template, an asynchronous review with a deadline, and a named reviewer, not a meeting for everyone.
Start with the people who are already persuaded, and measure something the sceptics care about.
followups: What would the one-page design template ask for, and why each item?
Two months in, reviews are rubber stamps: approved within an hour with no comments. What do you do?
Your most productive engineer refuses to write designs for their changes. How do you handle it?
How would you show the director, after a quarter, whether reviews were worth the time?
In your real example, what did the practice catch, what did it cost, and what did you change after trying it?

rules.ask: The team complies but resents it, and designs become box-ticking. How would you notice, and what would you change?
Which item on your checklist would have caught last quarter's incident, and how do you keep the checklist from growing forever?
Nine people in a one-hour meeting every week is a lot of time. What does it buy that an asynchronous review would not?
Fewer incidents could also be luck. What would convince you, and the sceptics, that reviews made the difference?
What did you do when your own first design got real criticism in review?

templates.title: A decision that has to be made this week on incomplete data
templates.subtopic: reversible and irreversible choices, risk, communication

deadline: the old pipeline's storage contract ends on Friday
the old pipeline runs on hosts that will be decommissioned on Friday
the old pipeline reads from a source table that is dropped on Friday
stake: the daily limit-consumption statement customer admins see
the usage figures account teams use in renewal conversations

sections.scenario: Your team has rebuilt the pipeline that computes per-org limit consumption, which drives {{stake}}. For three weeks the new pipeline has run in shadow beside the old one. For most orgs the two agree exactly, but for {{gap}} they differ by more than 1%, sometimes in one direction and sometimes in the other, and the team has explained only part of it (late events handled differently, and a time-zone boundary). The rest is not yet understood. You must decide this week whether to cut over, because {{deadline}}.
sections.problem: Walk me through how you make this decision. Cover what you do in the first day to narrow the unknowns; how you decide which unknowns matter; what options you consider beyond "cut over" and "do not cut over"; how you judge which errors are reversible and which are not; who you involve and who decides; how you communicate the decision and its risks; and what you put in place to catch a wrong call quickly. Then tell me about a real time you made an important technical decision with incomplete information, and how it turned out, or say you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The deadline cannot move. Customers are not told about pipeline changes unless something they see changes. The team is tired after three weeks of comparisons.
sections.assumptions: The pipelines, figures and deadline are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Frames the decision (what is decided, by whom, by when, what is at stake for {{stake}}); narrows the unknowns fast by grouping the differing orgs and sizing the effect; separates reversible from irreversible parts and looks for options that preserve reversibility (cut over with the old results archived for comparison, phased cutover, holding back the uncertain group, a manual check before anything customer-visible); sets explicit reversal triggers and monitoring; involves the right people without diffusing ownership; communicates the decision, the evidence and the residual risk plainly; looks after a tired team; real example with what was known, the decision, the outcome and the lesson, or an honest hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Which pipeline is right when they differ?
clarifications.a: For the explained part, the new one. For the rest, nobody knows yet.

clarifications.q: Can both run for a while longer?
clarifications.a: Not as they are: the deadline is fixed. Keeping part of the old pipeline running a little longer might be possible, at a cost you would have to justify.

clarifications.q: Who owns the decision?
clarifications.a: You do, as the technical lead; your director will back you if the reasoning is clear.

clarifications.q: Do the differing orgs have anything in common?
clarifications.a: Unknown. Nobody has looked at them as a group yet.

hints: Separate what you must know to decide from what you would like to know. Group the differing orgs before investigating them one by one.
Look for options that make the decision more reversible: cut over with a fallback, cut over for most orgs, or keep the old result for the uncertain group.
Decide what would make you reverse the decision, and set that up before you make it.
followups: In the first day, what analysis would you run on the differing orgs, and why that first?
What options exist between cutting over everything and cutting over nothing, and what does each cost?
You cut over. On day two, one large org's statement is 4% higher than it would have been under the old pipeline, and their admin asks why. What do you do?
How would you explain the decision and its residual risk to your director in five sentences?
In your real example, what did you know, what did you not, and what would you do differently with hindsight?

rules.ask: The deadline cannot move. What exactly happens on that day if you have not decided, and is that better or worse than deciding?
For how long can you roll back after the old pipeline is gone, and what would trigger it?
Which part of the difference is still unexplained, and how did you weigh it?
Who made the final call, and how did you handle the engineer who disagreed?
Customers are not told about pipeline changes unless something they see changes. Does something they see change here, and how do you know?

templates.title: Stepping back from being the team's best debugger so others can grow
templates.subtopic: delegation, knowledge sharing, on-call ownership, removing yourself as a bottleneck

system: the asynchronous job platform that runs customers' queued and scheduled work
the pipeline that records automation runs, faults and timings for customer admins
the identity resolution service that builds unified customer profiles

sections.scenario: You know {{system}} better than anyone; you wrote much of it. In the last six months you were pulled into {{share}} of its serious incidents, usually within minutes of the page, and you usually found the cause fast. Your manager says the team of {{team}} has stopped trying: on-call engineers escalate to you almost immediately. Two engineers have told you they would like to get better at debugging the system but feel there is no point while you are around. You are also needed on a new design that leadership cares about.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you change your own behaviour during incidents; how you transfer what you know (and what in your head is not written down); how you let others debug without putting customers at risk; how you decide when to step in; and how you know the team is getting better. Then tell me about a real time you deliberately made yourself less needed, or a time you were the bottleneck, and what happened, or say you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Customers' incidents still need to be resolved quickly. You cannot simply stop answering pages overnight. Your manager wants you on the new design within a quarter.
sections.assumptions: The team, system and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Recognises the bottleneck as partly their own behaviour; changes their incident role to coach with clear, pre-agreed rules for taking over based on customer impact; turns tacit knowledge into artefacts (a debugging guide, dashboards, saved queries, a failure-mode catalogue, recorded walk-throughs) owned by others; uses game days or replays of past incidents for practice; measures progress (share of incidents resolved without them, time to resolve, escalations); protects customers while accepting some short-term cost; handles a slower incident honestly; gives others visible credit; real example with what they changed in themselves and the result, or an honest hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there a runbook?
clarifications.a: A short one, out of date. Most knowledge is in your head and in old chat threads.

clarifications.q: Are the other engineers capable?
clarifications.a: Yes. They are strong engineers who have not had the chance to build the mental model.

clarifications.q: Do incidents take longer when you are not involved?
clarifications.a: On the few occasions it happened, about twice as long.

clarifications.q: Does your manager support slower incident resolution for a while?
clarifications.a: Within limits: no customer-visible incident may run much longer because of it.

hints: Change your role in incidents from solver to coach: ask the questions you would ask yourself, out loud, and let the on-call engineer drive.
Turn your debugging into artefacts: how you narrow a problem, the dashboards and queries you use, the failure modes you have seen.
Agree in advance on when you take over, so the decision is not made in the heat of an incident.
followups: The next page comes in at 14:00 and you can see the likely cause within two minutes. What do you do?
What exactly would you write down or build first so that others can debug {{system}} without you?
How would you measure, after a quarter, whether the team has become less dependent on you?
An incident goes badly while you are coaching: it runs 40 minutes longer than it would have with you driving. What do you tell your manager and the team?
In your real example, what did it cost you to step back, and what did the people who grew do with the room you gave them?

rules.ask: Runbooks go stale as fast as the code changes. How do you keep yours true, and who owns it once you step back?
Shadowing shows what you do but not why. How do you make your reasoning visible while you debug?
What is your rule for taking over, and did you agree it with the team before the incident or in the middle of it?
The on-call rotation includes engineers who joined last month. How do you make their first incident a learning one rather than a frightening one?
In that example, who else could have found it, and what would it have taken for them to?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for multi-tenant enterprise CRM
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, tenant isolation and per-tenant limits

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: each tenant's data kept strictly apart, including in caches, logs and analytics
each tenant limited so one cannot slow the others down
each tenant able to add its own fields and objects without a code change
each tenant's data kept in a region the tenant chooses

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if it served {{tenants}} of customer organisations from shared infrastructure, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes if the system served {{tenants}} of tenants with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The multi-tenant setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible multi-tenant analysis that starts from the tenant id in every key and query path, names the single-customer assumptions, and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example tenant-scoped keys with enforcement in the data-access layer and tests that prove it, per-tenant quotas and fair scheduling sized to tenant skew, metadata-driven custom fields stored as data rather than per-tenant schemas, tenant placement by region with routing and residency checks); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a multi-tenant system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the multi-tenant part is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the multi-tenant question, start from the tenant id: where it enters, which keys and indexes carry it, and which shared resource it does not yet bound.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design assume a single customer? What breaks first with {{tenants}} of tenants?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
With {{tenants}} of tenants, what does a schema migration look like, and how long does it take to reach the last one?
Show me the one place where a query could forget the tenant id. What stops it reaching another tenant's rows?
One tenant is a thousand times larger than the median. Does your limit fit both, and who sets it?
